blocks.text: World·New

Russian forces hammered energy infrastructure around Ukraine's capital with missiles and drones overnight, straining Kyiv's power supply and heating systems as temperatures headed toward zero, officials said on Saturday.
Explosions rocked the capital as Russia fired multiple waves of ballistic missiles
Explosions rocked the city as Russia fired multiple waves of ballistic missiles, several of which hit and damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Strikes on energy facilities outside Kyiv — including systems sending power from two nuclear plants to the city and Ukraine's central regions — caused serious damage, the Ministry of Energy said.
What can Canadian defence firms learn from Ukraine's drone expertise?

"The capital is facing serious difficulties with its electricity, water, and heat supplies," President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media platform X, adding that substations in five other regions were also hit.
He said Russia launched 36 ballistic missiles, only four of which were intercepted, according to Ukraine's air force. It added that air defences had downed 149 out of 172 drones.
At least two people killed
At least two people were killed and about a dozen others wounded across Ukraine in the overnight attacks, which also damaged homes, businesses and non-residential buildings, authorities said.

Moscow's Defence Ministry said it carried out a massive strike on what it described as targets in Ukraine's military-industrial sector, as well as energy and transport infrastructure in and around Kyiv.

It has expanded its campaign in recent weeks to target Kyiv's bridges, snarling traffic in the city of more than three million people.
B.C. animal rescuer killed by drone on Ukraine's front lines
Saturday's strikes come days before a new round of three-way talks in Abu Dhabi between Ukrainian and Russian officials, as part of a U.S.-backed peace push that has so far yielded few results.
"Russia is preparing for trilateral talks by launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine's critical infrastructure," Zelenskyy said on X.

items: Ukraine, Russia both say they were hit by cyberattacks

articles.title: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.summary:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro

Volodymyr Zelenskyy

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.

Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.

Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.

The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.

The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.

They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.

In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion

Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.

Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”

Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.

Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title: Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller a middle finger to millions of voters
articles.summary:
Architect of Trump’s far-right immigration agenda is now most powerful unelected figure in government – it suggests White House is moving to a war footing

Donald Trump just gave the middle…

blocks.text: Donald Trump just gave the middle finger to millions of American voters.

Any other president who suffered the kind of drubbing at the polls that Trump did this week might have felt at least a sliver of humility – and perhaps even an obligation to work with the new opposition in Congress.

But not for the first time in his political career, Trump veered in the opposite direction. On Friday he made Stephen Miller, condemned by Democrats and civil rights groups as a white nationalist, one of the most powerful unelected officials in Washington by naming him White House chief of staff.

Miller is the architect of Trump’s far-right, nativist immigration agenda. He is, therefore, arguably the architect of the blue wave that engulfed Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters – including many Latinos – expressed their disgust. Yet instead of firing Miller, Trump promoted him.

It was a declaration of war. Miller, 41, is a longtime proponent of the presidential authority that Trump has spent the past two years expanding at the expense of Congress. In 2017 he declared: “The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.”
Now Republicans’ catastrophic defeat is likely to leave Trump more reliant on unilateral executive action than ever to advance his domestic agenda.

“In a lot of ways Stephen Miller has been the id to Trump’s authoritarian impulses and machinations,” Kurt Bardella, an adviser to Democrats in Texas, said. “I have to imagine that anointing this person chief of staff – the most powerful non-elected position in all of government – is a signal that they intend to double down on that authoritarianism.
“You’re going to see a lot of executive orders, unilateral action and stress testing of the checks and balances system continue for the final two years of his presidency.”

Trump’s second term has presented a concerted effort to dismantle those checks and balances that have traditionally constrained the occupant of the White House. He has signed 292 executive orders in less than two years, more than in his entire first term and a record pace for a modern presidency.

He has bypassed Congress on military action and tariffs, withheld congressionally approved spending, deployed the National Guard against the will of state authorities, politicised the justice department, punished critics and challenged judicial independence. Congress, dominated by Republicans reluctant to confront him, offered little resistance.

But this week’s landslide, the biggest in a midterm election since Watergate, puts Democrats back in charge of the House of Representatives and Senate. That the elections were free and fair, and that Trump did not dispute the result, was itself a victory for democracy.

Democrats will now seek to rein in the president and block his legislative agenda, bringing them into direct conflict with Miller, who was already a hugely powerful deputy chief of staff at the White House and now takes over from Susie Wiles.

Miller has been a champion of the Iran war and prominent voice on many of the president’s other priorities, including countering diversity initiatives and targeting transgender rights. He is reportedly one of a small group of White House staffers who approve all executive orders.

He is best known for driving the ‌immigration crackdown in Trump’s second term, setting ‌a target of 3,000 arrests per day – far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to target anybody in ‌the country illegally, not just those with criminal records.

There are limits on what Democrats can do to stop the immigration drive since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included major increases for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that will keep it funded for the rest of Trump’s term.

Even so, they will now chair House committees with the ability to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and hold high profile hearings. Along with ICE, they might scrutinise Jeffrey Epstein files and the department of government efficiency (Doge). They have also vowed to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.

The appointment of the pugnacious Miller as Trump’s consigliere suggests that the White House is moving to a war footing. He is likely to marshal a team of lawyers and attack Democrats by accusing them of weaponising the deep state against the president. As a frequent guest on the conservative Fox News network, he will also wage war in the court of public opinion.

“Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller means that he’s spoiling for a fight with Democrats and they’re going to just rely on executive action to try and push their agenda through,” said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron in Ohio, who studies the American presidency and White House staffing.

Cohen added: “It’s a White House that doesn’t seek out cooperation with Congress. It’s their way or the highway, essentially, and it’s possible Stephen Miller is relishing this because he’s a believer in the unitary presidency and executive presidential action and he views this as a way where he can expand the powers of the presidency.”

Trump is not the first president to seek to consolidate authority. Arthur Schlesinger Jr’s 1973 book The Imperial Presidency warned that an accumulation of presidential power threatened the constitutional separation of powers.

In 1989 the American Enterprise Institute thinktank published The Fettered Presidency, a counterpoint arguing that legal and congressional constraints had unduly weakened the executive. It helped inspire a modern conservative drive to expand presidential authority, which accelerated under George W Bush and was subsequently exploited by Barack Obama as congressional gridlock made legislating increasingly difficult.
The combination of Trump and Miller, however, takes the concept of an American Caesar to a new extreme – and flies in the face of the verdict delivered by the electorate on Tuesday.

“It’s a step that I find hard to fathom except as the president giving the middle finger to the American public,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington.
“In the same way that he ransacked the state of Texas for the very worst senatorial nominee imaginable, now he’s done the same thing with the chief of staff position. This is simply outrageous.”

articles.title: Court rules against Home Office in asylum seeker kidnapping case
articles.summary:
Department had claimed that being kidnapped for ransom was not exploitation of trafficking victims in case of Syrian man abducted in Libya

The court of appeal has rejected claims by the Home…

blocks.text: The court of appeal has rejected claims by the Home Office that being kidnapped for ransom is not exploitation of trafficking victims.

The ruling means that many people who have been kidnapped for ransom, whom officials have previously excluded from being victims of exploitation under trafficking rules, will now have to have these claims considered. They may be eligible for the support and recovery package trafficking victims are entitled to.

Being kidnapped for ransom is a common hazard for asylum seekers passing through Libya on their journey to Europe. Many are fleeing conflict in countries such as Sudan and Eritrea as well as some Middle Eastern countries.

The legal challenge was brought by a Syrian asylum seeker who cannot be identified. The 25-year-old fled forced military conscription in July 2021, knowing he was likely to be imprisoned and tortured in Syria for refusing to fight.

He arrived in Libya, ultimately hoping to reach the UK. He and other Syrians were abducted by armed men and held in captivity for a month between August and September 2021. His money and phone were seized and they were driven through the desert for 24 hours, hearing gunshots, with no food and little water.

They were told they would not be released until their families agreed to pay a ransom of several thousand dollars. He was tied up and often beaten on his hands and feet by his kidnappers. He and the other captives had to phone their families to beg them to pay their kidnappers the ransom money. While they were on the phone, the kidnappers beat them so their families could hear screams. He was terrified that even if his family paid his captors, he might not be released and that his organs might be harvested.

The man was released after his family paid his kidnappers, and he made his way to Europe, crossing the Mediterranean from Libya to Italy by boat. He crossed the Channel from France to the UK on 16 May 2022 and claimed asylum.

The Home Office rejected his trafficking claim, arguing that because he had not been subjected to forced labour by his kidnappers, his experience did not meet the definition of exploitation in the trafficking rules. He challenged the decision in the high court, which ruled in his favour. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, appealed against the ruling.

While the government has pledged to support trafficking victims, the decision to exclude asylum seekers kidnapped for ransom in Libya has denied many the support the judges ruled they may be entitled to. Recent freedom of information data relating to asylum seekers who were confirmed to be genuine trafficking victims found that of the 1,778 confirmed victims between July 2024 and July 2025, 89% were forcibly removed from the UK, putting them at risk of being trafficked again.

While each trafficking claim must be considered on the facts of the individual case, the judgment found: “The secretary of state erred in not considering the question of whether kidnapping amounted to exploitation.”

The ruling could help thousands of potential trafficking victims, not only those who arrive in Britain in the future but also those previously rejected as being trafficking victims who were kidnapped and held to ransom in Libya. They can now get a fresh referral into the national referral mechanism for a new decision on whether there are reasonable grounds for them to be considered a victim of trafficking.
after newsletter promotion

Jeremy Bloom, a consultant solicitor at Duncan Lewis, who represented the Syrian man, welcomed the ruling. “This judgment is a vindication of my client’s claim to be a victim of trafficking. The Home Office sought to restrict the definition of exploitation,” he said.

“We hope that it will also assist other victims of trafficking who have experienced similarly horrendous treatment to gain access to the leave and support that they need to recover from those experiences. Those individuals may include people who have had their claims to be a victim of trafficking refused, and who might now be able to ask for a new decision based on the law as set out in this judgment.”

Home Office sources said it would not be appropriate to comment on legal proceedings. A Home Office spokesperson said:“We are simplifying and strengthening protection and immigration routes, ensuring they are clear, targeted and focused on their intended purpose, while maintaining fairness and public confidence.”

articles.title: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

blocks.text: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhihia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title: Two men arrested after boy injured in Gloucester sword attack
articles.summary:
Armed police attended the scene, which led to two nearby schools going into lockdown on Friday

Two teenagers have been arrested after a 17-year-old was injured in a suspected sword attack…

blocks.text: Two teenagers have been arrested after a 17-year-old was injured in a suspected sword attack near a Catholic school in Gloucester.

Officers were called to Chalford Road, near St Peter’s high school, in Tuffley, shortly after 8.50am on Friday. It was reported that two men – one in possession of a sword – had been seen chasing two 17-year-old boys. The suspects then fled the scene on foot.
One of the victims sustained a “superficial wound believed to have been caused by the sword”, Gloucestershire constabulary have said. The other boy involved was not physically injured.
Armed police attended the scene to search for the suspects. St Peter’s high school and the nearby Willow primary academy were put on lockdown on Friday after the incident.
A 19-year-old man was arrested overnight, while an 18-year-old handed himself in to the police on Saturday morning. Both of the men are from Gloucester and remain in police custody for questioning.
Police said a woman had been arrested on Friday on suspicion of assisting an offender, but was released on police bail pending further inquiries.

A pupil named Jimmy at St Peter’s high school told the BBC that the situation was “really scary”, and students were locked in their classrooms for several hours. “At the time I was scared,” he said. “My heart was racing.”

Parents also received messages from the secondary school, explaining there had been an incident but that the situation was under control. DI Sophie Dawkins, from the constabulary’s CID, said: “We completely understand the concern this incident would have caused, especially when it happened near a school at drop off time.
“We’ve had armed officers searching the area, along with support from our drone unit and the National Police Air Service, and work is ongoing to identify and locate those involved.
after newsletter promotion
“Numerous inquiries have been taking place and officers from the neighbourhood team have been in the area throughout the day to reassure parents that there is not thought to be a wider threat.
“We are now keen to hear from anyone who has not already spoken to police who witnessed what happened or who has dashcam or any other footage.”

articles.title: Alex Eala survives Greek opponent, rain-hit Hong Kong semis for title berth
articles.summary: Filipina tennis superstar and world No. 17 Alex Eala keeps up her torrid surge through the 2026 Hong Kong Open, this time surviving Greek veteran Maria Sakkari in the semis to arrange a final match…

blocks.text: HIT. Filipina tennis star Alex Eala in action at the 2026 Hong Kong Open.
HONG KONG OPEN

Filipina tennis superstar and world No. 17 Alex Eala keeps up her torrid surge through the 2026 Hong Kong Open, this time surviving Greek veteran Maria Sakkari in the semis to arrange a final match against Claire Liu
MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala closes in on her first WTA 250 title as she survived Greek veteran Maria Sakkari, 7-5, 3-6, 6-4, in the 2026 Hong Kong Open semifinals on Saturday, November 7.
World No. 102 American Claire Liu now stands in the way of the world No. 17 Filipina superstar in the final, after her own 7-5, 6-4 semifinal sweep of Russian challenger Alexandra Shubladze.
Reeling from a 3-6 setback in the second set, Eala aimed to exorcise ghosts of meltdowns past with a blazing 3-0 start in the final frame, and kept a huge 4-1 advantage with the final within grasp.

The 31-year-old Sakkari, however, refused to go down without a fight as she staged her own clutch three-game rally to stage a 4-4 tie, before Eala stopped the bleeding in the ninth game, giving up only a single point to go up 5-4.
Perhaps running out of gas late, Sakkari failed to keep up with Eala’s final onslaught, only saving one match point in the end as the Filipina ace wrapped up another hard-earned three-set victory.

Ahead of the final, Eala also aims to avenge an earlier upset loss, as Liu — then ranked world No. 305 — stunned the top-50 Filipina out of the 2025 Guangzhou Open first round in their only head-to-head meeting so far.

Regardless of result, the Hong Kong Open will be Eala’s final official event of the year as she soon heads home for a wind-down homecoming celebration at the sprawling Philippine Arena on December 8. – Rappler.com

articles.title: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to lower birth weight, study finds
articles.summary:
Dinch, an allegedly ‘safe’ alternative, used in the EU and US also found to cause fetal development complications

Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to…

blocks.text: Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found.

As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety”, nontoxic alternative. It is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children’s toys, medical devices, some textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.

But it may not be as safe as industry has claimed, the New York University Langone Health analysis of federal US health data suggests. There is a dearth of research into Dinch health risks, though what exists points toward the chemicals being hormone disruptors that can impact kids’ development.

The new paper is the first to link Dinch to lower birth weights and birth lengths. Fetal growth problems can raise the risk for heart disease, learning difficulties, obesity and other issues that can echo into adolescence and adulthood, the authors wrote.
“Chemicals should be properly tested for their safety before they become a widespread exposure for unwitting people in the general public,” said Leonardo Trasande, a lead author on the NYU paper.

The chemical is formally named 1,2-cyclohexane dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester. It is used to make plastic more flexible and durable, and is found in common kitchen products such as cling film and plastic wine corks.

Researchers looked at data for over 6,600 pregnancies collected as part of the National Institutes of Health Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (Echo) Program. Up to 70% of women showed Dinch in their urine, and higher levels increased the risk of the child being classified as “small for gestational age”, or below the 10th percentile for babies born at the same stage of pregnancy.

Each tenfold increase in Dinch exposure resulted in a 27-gram reduction in newborn birth weight. An average newborn weighs about 3,400 grams (about 7.5lbs). Hispanic mothers or those with lower education levels were more likely to have children affected by Dinch, the study found.

Previous research on animals and human cells has found that Dinch by-products can interfere with the hormones in a pregnant woman that guide fetal development, and may trigger inflammation that affects how nutrients and oxygen reach the baby, NYU’s authors wrote.

The paper appears to expose yet another classic example of industry replacing one dangerous chemical with a compound that has similar health effects. This resets the regulatory and research process, even though the new chemical is very similar in structure or has the same health risks.

After the US and EU regulators began taking action in the aughts over toxic phthalates such as DEHP, industry began increasing the use of Dinch. German chemical giant BASF is among Dinch’s major producers and overall global production volume jumped from 25,000 tons in 2002 to 400,000 tons in 2024.

This process is called “regrettable substitution”, and is common. For example, many chemical companies and goods producers replaced the most dangerous Pfas “forever chemicals”, such as Pfoa, with GenX compounds. But after years of research, the latter have been found to be more toxic.

Researchers with the Switzerland-based Food Packaging Forum said they are concerned about Dinch and the lack of health information around it. But there is evidence that it migrates from food packaging into food, and levels in the EU population have been increasing across recent decades. The Food Packaging Forum is currently conducting health research on DINCH.
The NYU findings “raise pretty serious concerns about regrettable substitution”, Trasande said.

“These results underscore the need for stronger oversight of chemicals used in food packaging and other household products by requiring they be tested before they are introduced to the market, instead of after they are connected to health concerns,” Trasande said, noting that the plastics treaty under negotiation at the United Nations is an opportunity to establish better policies.

Women can protect themselves and their children by buying plastic-free products as much as possible, including clothing and toys. Look for food at the grocery store that comes in glass packaging, and use glass or wood storage and utensils in the kitchen.

articles.title: Florida Republicans survived the ‘blue wave’, but find themselves on shaky ground
articles.summary:
Sunshine state emerged as the lone flag bearer of the Maga agenda, but even there, the GOP finds itself on the defense

After the dust settled on Tuesday night’s near-annihilation of the…

blocks.text: After the dust settled on Tuesday night’s near-annihilation of the Republican party nationwide, a single red flag fluttered defiantly in Florida, now a last bastion of the Maga movement that has dominated politics in the US for a decade.

Voters in the Sunshine state bucked the national trend, just barely, to elect two close allies of Donald Trump into office: congressman Byron Donalds as its first Black governor, and Ashley Moody to the US Senate.

But it was a close call – both margins of victory under 3% – and the shockwaves created metaphorical cracks in the stucco of Mar-a-Lago, the president’s prized citadel by the sea, if not the walls themselves.

Only a generation ago, Florida was the ultimate swing state, but turned reliably red in recent years to become a stronghold of conservatism. From here, Trump plotted his remarkable political comeback from the wilderness of his 2020 defeat to Joe Biden, and the ashes of the January 6 riots.
As well as being Trump’s home, Florida is where Ron DeSantis, the outgoing right-wing governor, molded so many of the policies expanded nationwide by the president during his second administration.

Attacks on LGBTQ+ communities; an aggressive, taxpayer-funded immigration crackdown and assaults on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), especially in higher education, were all weaned in the Sunshine state, bolstered by DeSantis’s ultra-loyal legislature that acquiesced to his whims at every turn.
Now, Florida finds itself facing something of a political retrenchment, as Trump’s power wanes on the national stage, and Republicans in the state reflect on a near-disaster.
The narrow victories of Donalds and Moody were certainly something for them to celebrate, especially against the stunning backdrop of Democratic upsets in South Carolina, Texas, Ohio, and elsewhere.

But it’s hard to escape the feeling that even here, where the president will doubtless spend substantial chunks of time playing golf during the final two years of what is now a lame-duck presidency, Maga’s last stand will be much less potent.

Analysts say that being Republican flag bearers in a lonely new political era, in which rejuvenated Florida Democrats are unexpectedly snapping at their heels again, will bring an unfamiliar range of challenges and risks.

Trump loyalist Donalds, for example, will not enjoy the same fealty from the Republican-controlled legislature that the termed-out DeSantis did, potentially checking the advancement of his own ultra-conservative agenda and promise to build on his predecessor’s legacy. Democrats made a net gain of 15 house seats in the state to strip the party’s supermajority.
“It’s unlikely he’ll have the clout that DeSantis had in his prime,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida.

“DeSantis really was almost all-powerful, getting almost anything he wanted. I don’t think that’s going to be the case with Donalds. He has presented himself as super Maga, he was all about the Maga agenda. Now he’s in office he might not push it quite as much, if for no other reason than Trump himself is in a severely weakened position.”

One element of Florida’s political make-up that did not change this week, but which was engineered to, was the number of Republicans elected to the US House of Representatives. An aggressive mid-cycle gerrymandering by DeSantis failed to work, with Democrats capturing all four districts (out of Florida’s 28) that were redrawn to disadvantage them, and holding four others.

“In this election cycle at least, it was a wash, a failed effort by Republicans,” Jewett said. “Democrats were able to fight it to a standstill and avoid losses. In the next election the fight will continue.”
Florida’s Democratic leaders celebrated those successes. “Florida voters saw through the blatant power grab,” the state party said Wednesday in a post on X.
DeSantis, at a press conference the same day, characterized the nationwide Republican wipeout as “close to an extinction-level event”, and took credit for Florida “holding the line”.

Florida Democrats, he said, had reached a high-water mark. “The question is, if you couldn’t win in this year, what circumstances are going to create the opportunity for you to win statewide in Florida?” he said.

“Florida is the last main anchor standing. Everyone that was on that ballot can look at Florida and then compare it to the rest of the country and know that there was a reason why we were able to withstand the worst of circumstances here.”
Jewett agreed with some of DeSantis’s reasoning. “Florida is a red state, there’s no doubt about it, but there are different shades of red,” he said.

“It’s not Wyoming red, where their senator won by like 65%. But the counterargument would be that Republicans always win, and that’s kind of the narrative for some of the national Democrats: ‘How many times are we going to say to ourselves if we just invest a little more and do a little more, we could win.’ And it just doesn’t happen.”

It’s an observation that resonates strongly with Democrats in the state. Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic party, told a press conference on Wednesday: “[We] are looking at the results across the country and can only imagine what kind of day we would be having if we had sustained national support.”

Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist, former labor organizer and state representative who lost to Moody after running on a shoestring-budget, grassroots campaign, with no television advertisements, concurred.
“Imagine what would have happened if we had more investment early on,” she said in a post on X shortly after her narrow defeat was confirmed.

Nixon lost by 2.9% in a seat most recently won by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, in the 2022 Senate election by more than 16%. Young voters, Hispanics and Black voters in particular came out in droves to support her, but she was massively disadvantaged in fundraising and spending, and financial support from national Democrats was too little, too late.
Nixon, however, said she is getting straight back to work.
“I’m proud of the race we ran. We helped drive turnout and broke the super majority in the state house and senate. 2028 is around the corner,” she said. “LFG! [let’s fucking go].”

articles.title: He quit firefighting for his mental health. Then he came to the rescue after a horrific bus crash
articles.summary: A lonely highway, a traumatized son, and up to 20 people in need of urgent care after a horrific bus crash: that's the situation Rich Rogers found himself in Wednesday morning along Highway 39, just…

image.caption: Rich Rogers was first on the scene in the aftermath of a major bus crash that sent 20 people to hospital the morning of Nov. 4, 2026, near Mackenzie, B.C. (Corynn Rogers/RCMP)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Q&A

A lonely highway, a traumatized son, and up to 20 people in need of urgent care after a horrific bus crash: that's the situation Rich Rogers found himself in Wednesday morning along Highway 39, just south of Mackenzie, B.C. A former firefighter, he spoke to reporters about the toll it can take and the importance of supporting first responders.
After springing into action to save lives, Rich Rogers speaks about the need to support first responders

A lonely highway, a traumatized son, and up to 20 people in need of urgent care after a horrific bus crash: that's the situation Rich Rogers found himself in Wednesday morning along Highway 39, just south of Mackenzie, B.C.
A former firefighter, he gave immediate life-saving treatment to the injured passengers until more help could arrive, reopening the mental trauma he tried to leave behind in his old career.
"Before I could blink Rich was running out of our car, down the steep bank and onto that bus," his wife Corynn wrote online.
"He didn't know what he would see in there, and I don't truly want to know all the details. I do know he literally saved several lives."
About 20 people hospitalized after bus crash near Mackenzie

As she frantically tried to call 911 in an area with poor cell coverage, Corynn says her husband turned off the bus as it was filling with gas, checked for pulses and revived people who were unconscious.

It took six ambulances, five airplanes, and a helicopter to respond to the crisis, which resulted in a Code Orange being declared at the hospitals in both Mackenzie and Prince George, roughly 200 kilometres south of the scene.

items: 15 patients released, 5 still hospitalized following bus crash near Mackenzie, B.C.
Hospital helipad could be 'difference between life and death,' union says after northern B.C. bus crash

blocks.text: But at first it was just Rogers, his family and the people in need of immediate care on an otherwise desolate northern highway.
Corynn says it was a miracle that her husband, a former City of Prince George firefighter, was the person who was there to treat the injured passengers before more help could arrive.
Corrine and Rich Rogers, along with their son, were the only other people on the road when the bus crashed into a ditch after driving toward them. (Corrine Rogers)

But the experience was also traumatic for Rogers, who left the job due to concerns about his mental health. Dealing with the aftermath of Wednesday's experience, he requested to conduct a single interview with multiple media outlets, including CBC News, via an online video call from his home in Mackenzie, where he moved in September.
A key message was the impact such situations can have on those who jump into help, and the need to support first responders.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Describe what you saw for us when you were going down Highway 39.

It was kind of surreal. We kind of came around a little bit of a corner into a fairly big straight away in the distance as we were talking, I noticed something weird and the fact that the bus kind of started entering our lane, and it didn't appear to be for any particular reason.
And then everything went into ultra-slow motion and I started slowing down. I could just feel and I could tell that something was about to happen.
LISTEN | Rogers shares his story:
Radio West9:51Witness account of shuttle bus crash near Mackenzie

At one point I thought they were gonna flip onto the highway on its side, but it seemed to just take off and shoot across the road and, unfortunately, on that that side of the road there was about a 20-foot-deep ditch.
They launched off the edge, for lack of a better word, and crashed into a tree and then the bus spun around and fell into the ditch and came to a stop.
During that time, my son and wife were in the vehicle with me, and my boy [his 12-year-old son] just started screaming "No, no, no," over and over.
Rogers says his focus moving forward will be on helping his son recover from what they witnessed, as well as making sure he is looking after his own mental health. (Corrine Rogers)

I pulled over into the side road and I told my family just to stay put and to call for help. And I can't even remember if I said it out loud, or if it was just in my head, "Man, I hope the bus is empty."
Rogers says one person had been ejected from the bus and they didn't appear to be breathing, so he started applying lifesaving measures and they started breathing again.

Another passenger who was hurt but mobile helped stabilize this person while Rogers moved onto to other injuries. B.C. Emergency Health Services confirms that three people were in serious condition while four others were in "serious but stable" condition.
Once ambulances arrived, Rogers continued to help until the scene was cleared.
This is obviously really hard.
I mean, part of the reason that I'm not a firefighter is I left due to mental stress.
So, yeah, it was a trying experience that we just went through but it's kind of reminded me and made me thankful for the training that I did have and possessed.

It's really tough. I went through a lot of emotional stress. I feel that I didn't get the support and the help that I deserved. I didn't know how to ask for it properly, either. And I don't know that I was ready to ask for it.

My wife recognized it in me before I did, that I was struggling. And we're definitely going to have to watch for those types of emotions and feelings creeping in again. But I believe that I'm more equipped to deal with those stressors now.
And how is your family navigating it?

The very first night my wife was extremely worried that my son wasn't going to be able to sleep because he just kept saying in the car ... that he all he could see is the bus keep crashing and crashing and crashing.

I'm thankful I was thoughtful enough to pull over about 100 meters away from the incident. In the back of my head I was thinking, "I don't want my kid and my wife to have to see what is, or potentially could be happening."
We just have to kind of make sure that he's not being negatively affected, and that he knows that we're here, that he can talk to us about whatever and anything that he needs to.
What kind of response have people been giving you?
I almost feel a little bit embarrassed because, honestly, doing this with you guys is harder for me than what I did.
I don't really think of myself as a hero, I just think of myself as the wrong place, right time, right skills.
I just hope what I did can give those guys a chance to get healthy again, a chance for their family to spend some time [together].

Rogers says it's important for first responders to receive support for the mental and emotional trauma they endure. He says he's grateful he may have helped more people have more time with their family. (Corrine Rogers)
I think the only thing that people should know is there's lots of people out there that would do what I did.
I think people need to respect the fact that when somebody says they're hurting inside, and they can't explain it, that it should be taken a little bit more seriously.
Like, I know my life would be a lot different right now if I was still still a firefighter.
I thought it was my dream career [and it] just destroyed my life.
But I have to move forward in my life, just like the people that were injured in that accident, and just do the best that I can from here for a while.

articles.title: New Zealand election too close to call with over 95% of votes counted
articles.summary: Initial results in New Zealand show the two main parties neck-and-neck with fewer than 4,000 votes separating them. Official results aren't expected until later this month once special votes have…

image.caption: Incumbent Luxon said his National Party has a 'pathway' to forming a governmentImage: David Rowland/REUTERS

blocks.text: The two main parties were effectively deadlocked in New Zealand's close-fought general elections on Saturday, with the rising cost of living and general economic problems the main issues at stake.
Results with 95% votes counted showed the ruling center-right National Party and the opposition Labour Party neck-and-neck with just under 30% of the vote.
The National Party held a slim lead of about 3,500 votes more than Labour late on Saturday night.
PM claims 'pathway' to power as opposition calls for 'common ground'
Incumbent Prime Minister Cristopher Luxon, who heads the National Party, said that his party "is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government."

The National Party currently governs in coalition with the pro-business ACT and the right-wing populist New Zealand First. According to preliminary results, the three parties are set to net a total 67 seats in parliament, amounting to a wafer-thin majority.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said that New Zealand's politicians would need to find "common ground" after the results showed neither his party nor the ruling National Party were likely to form a governing majority on their own.
"New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said," Hipkins told supporters.
"Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground."

blocks.caption: Hipkins served as PM for 10 months after succeeding Jacinda Ardern in 2023Image: Yuxin Liu/AFP

blocks.text: What to know about the election results in New Zealand

Special votes, including those cast from people overseas, are to be counted over the next three weeks. The votes typically benefit left-leaning parties and have shifted preliminary election results over the last three elections.
Final results are expected to be released on November 27.

If the right-wing bloc fails to hold on to its slim majority, the centrist Opportunity Party could act as a kingmaker. The party is projected to get seven seats, putting it past the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time since it was founded in 2017.
Luxon has previously ruled out cooperating with the Opportunity Party.
New Zealand has a mixed-member proportional system that requires voters to tick two options: a party and a local electoral candidate.

Electorate winners earn a seat in parliament, which typically has 120 seats, unless a so-called "overhang" leads to more lawmakers being returned to parliament, along with the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

blocks.caption: New Zealand's parliament sits in WellingtonImage: picture-alliance/M.Moritz

blocks.text: Preliminary results on Saturday showed that parliament is set to expand to 130 seats because of the overhang, making it the largest parliament in New Zealand history.
The vote took against a backdrop of high prices for basic goods and the highest unemployment in more than a decade.
The voting took place under New Zealand's strict laws banning media reporting and political campaigning on the final day.

New Zealanders have, however, been able to cast their votes since October 26, with almost 1.7 million of the country's 3.8 million eligible voters already casting their ballots by Thursday, according to the electoral commission.

articles.title: Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia
articles.summary: International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's…

image.caption: The last time Russia competed at the IIHF World Hockey Championship was in December 2021 in Red Deer, AlbertaImage: Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.
Hosting Worlds 'practically impossible'

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."
Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.
German visa restrictions on Russians in place

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.
"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."
Consensus remains elusive
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

articles.title: No Pax Silica deal at ASEAN Summit, says US envoy
articles.summary: Pax Silica decisions ‘will be made in full consultation’ with the Philippines, says US Ambassador Lee Lipton ahead of the ASEAN Summit in Manila

blocks.text: HOST. The welcome sign at the entrance of the Philippine International Convention Center complex and World Trade Center in Pasay City, on November 4, 2026.
Rappler
Pax Silica decisions ‘will be made in full consultation’ with the Philippines, says US Ambassador Lee Lipton ahead of the ASEAN Summit in Manila

MANILA, Philippines – A United States envoy dismissed reports on Saturday, November 7, that a framework agreement for the US-backed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone would be signed during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila this month.

“No such announcement on the Pax Silica Economic Security Zone was ever planned. Decisions will be made in full consultation with the government of the Philippines at the appropriate time,” US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said in a statement.
“As stated previously and as part of this process, we expect rigorous discussions on impacts to all stakeholders.”

Lipton’s clarification came after the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) earlier floated that the signing of the initiative — which aims to transform the Philippines into a hub for artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, and advanced industries — could be among the major developments during the summit from November 16 to 18.
US President Donald Trump will be among the global leaders expected to attend the regional event.

Envisioned as a massive 1,620-hectare industrial hub in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, the Pax Silica development is estimated by the BCDA to attract up to US$70 billion in investments and create as many as 190,000 direct jobs.

The project, however, faces mounting criticisms in the Philippines, with many noting that the hub could harm the country’s environment, displace indigenous communities, and strain the Luzon energy grid because of its massive power and water needs, among others.

“We look forward to working alongside the government of the Philippines about this exciting initiative to secure supply chains and attract quality investment in support of economic growth and jobs at home for the people,” Lipton said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Watchdog, House speaker agree to work on budget transparency
articles.summary: The People"s Budget Coalition (PBC) commended House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III who expressed commitment to greater transparency in the national budget process, signifying a constructive…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 6:43pm
The People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) commended House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III who expressed commitment to "greater transparency" in the national budget process
This comes after the PBC met with Dy to discuss areas where the House could enhance its processes for scrutinizing and disclosing government projects.

“Thank you, Speaker Faustino ‘Bojie’ Dy III, for meeting with the People’s Budget Coalition... acknowledging the points for improvement in the House process, and committing to working with us budget watchdogs and civil society groups to open up these documents and deliberations so that every taxpayer can verify where our taxes go,” Abante said in a Facebook post.
His statement came after Dy said that the House was ready to disclose supporting documents for government projects and promote greater transparency in budget deliberations.

According to the civil society group, the development points to a significant shift toward constructive engagement between lawmakers and civil society organizations that have raised concerns about project documentation, technical descriptions and amendments in the proposed P6.793-trillion national budget for 2027.

The PBC said that instead of dismissing concerns raised by independent budget monitors, the House leadership has opened channels for dialogue and cooperation to reinforce public scrutiny of government expenditures.

To recall, Dy said the House of Representatives is open to disclosing supporting documents for government projects and make budget deliberations more accessible to the public, in order that proposed appropriations can be examined against their supporting studies, technical specifications, project locations and implementing agencies’ validation.
“Such disclosures would help distinguish properly documented and justified budget amendments from questionable allocations that require further scrutiny,” the PBC said.

The PBC added the House Speaker’s approach also backs the principle that government projects should be evaluated on their merits, supporting documentation and benefits to the public, instead of allegations alone. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: France braces for new round of Yellow Vest, student protests
articles.summary: Two major protests have been announced for Saturday. One will see students and unions marching against high living costs, while the Yellow Vests plan to march separately, despite a police ban.

image.caption: School students rallied again in Paris on FridayImage: Eric Baradat/REUTERS

blocks.text: France is bracing for its fourth weekend of mass demonstrations, as student protests over cost of living and the state of the country's schools show no sign of abating.
On Saturday afternoon, authorities say students and labor unions will take part in an authorized central Paris march "against the high cost of living and in support of young people."

Separately, the country's so-called "Yellow Vest" movement — which gained notoriety eight years ago by violently protesting a proposed fuel tax hike — has rejected invitations to join the student rally.
Instead, the Gilets Jaunes are calling for "mass disobedience" at a banned event at Paris' Place de la Concorde, close to parliament and the presidential Elysee Palace.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 70,000 police and security forces will be deployed across the country over the weekend, adding that authorities will "be ready" for "rioters and looters."
France protests turn violent nationwide
Can France afford to raise wages, invest in schools?

The large police presence comes on the heels of weeks of mass demonstrations that have at times grown extremely violent, most notably on October 17, when France's worst rioting in years resulted in more than a billion euros in damage to private and public property.
On Thursday, police made over 600 arrests during a nationwide strike that included blockades and other protest action.
Authorities say that, for the most part, protests have remained peaceful.

But there have continued to be numerous incidents of violent clashes with police, as outgoing President Emmanuel Macron and his government struggle to address public discontent over the rising cost of living.

Although Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is scheduled to meet with trade and employee unions on Monday, organizers say the only thing that will quell anger will be for the government to bow to their demands.

"The only thing that will bring the protests to an end is a response to the demands that have been put forward for several weeks by workers, civil servants, young people and pensioners," according to an inter-union coalition statement published on Friday.
This latest round of protests began with students calling for improvements to the national education system and unions joining in to call for wage hikes and tax reforms.

Macron's government has said it intends to raise the minimum wage as well as increase funding for schools and teaching staff. But it finds itself in a tight fiscal spot as debt — currently 119% of GDP — continues to run out of control in the EU's second-largest economy.
Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe?

articles.title: Ukraine: Russia hits Kyiv with airstrikes ahead of trilateral talks
articles.summary: The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi.

image.caption: Russian forces hit several sites across the Kyiv region overnightImage: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia launched strikes on Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said on Saturday.
Russia's Defense Ministry said the strikes hit the Northern Bridge and the Meridian Plant.
Moscow said that the bridge was being used by the Ukrainian military to transport weapons and military equipment, while the plant is used to produce Flamingo cruise missiles.
It said the strikes damaged several energy and industrial facilities in the Kyiv region, as well as an electricity substation in the neighboring Zhytomyr region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

blocks.caption: Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities as its ground offensive has stalledImage: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

blocks.text: What have Ukrainian authorities said about the attacks?

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the strikes on the Northern Bridge, adding that the Ukrainian capital found itself in an "extremely difficult" situation regarding power, heating and water supplies. Overnight temperatures dropped to 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) in the city.
The Kyiv region's governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said energy facilities in three of its districts had been hit.
Ukrainian authorities said that one person was killed and eight were wounded in the overnight attack.
In a statement on social media, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles during the attack.
He said that Russia was trying to "push Kyiv … and the entire country into a blackout" and repeated his call for increased support from the United States.
Russia has stepped up airstrikes on Ukraine in recent months, targeting energy infrastructure and major cities, and more recently hitting bridges.
Is Trump negotiating a new European security order with Russia?
Strikes come ahead of Russia-Ukraine talks
The strikes come days before a fourth round of trilateral talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates.
Previous rounds of US-brokered talks have failed to achieve any breakthroughs, with territorial and security questions remaining major points of contention.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump said the war could be close to being settled and that he envisioned a "big, beautiful agreement" with Moscow that involves "all of Europe."
Last Friday, a six-day local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region enabled the evacuation of some 800 residents.
The brief truce was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

articles.title: Home Office sued after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of right to live in UK
articles.summary:
Campaign group the3million lodges court papers after EU citizens told pre-settled status was an ‘error’

The Home Office is being sued for alleged breach of the Brexit withdrawal agreement…

blocks.text: The Home Office is being sued for alleged breach of the Brexit withdrawal agreement after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of their full rights to live in the UK.

Campaign group the3million lodged papers at the high court on Friday after several cases emerged of EU citizens who were granted pre-settled status to remain in the country after Brexit but were told recently those decisions were an “error”.

According to the statement of claim, the Home Office decision to remove all or some rights from citizens granted pre-settled status was made without “procedural protections” required under the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA).

These protections include a right of an appeal and an assessment of “proportionality”, which would establish whether removal of rights was appropriate given the EU citizens in question built their lives in the UK on the basis of the Home Office’s original decision.

Among the people affected by the Home Office policy was a 33-year-old Brazilian Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018. He was originally told that he should not have settled status: he could stay but his Brazilian wife could not, a decision that was reversed in the last few weeks after objections were raised.

Another EU citizen who raised her case with the3million is a woman working in the NHS and studying for a PhD in dentistry. She has said the Home Office’s notification had “turned her life upside down”.

In October 2026, the Home Office accepted that where a person provides evidence of their Italian citizenship, together with evidence that this was obtained through jure sanguinis, they would now accept that this person was an Italian from birth.

Previously it told a number of Brazilian Italians they were granted status “in error” because they had not presented an Italian passport at the time of their application, merely stating they were Italian citizens.

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, said: “The Home Office is putting the cart before the horse. It denies people the safeguards the withdrawal agreement guarantees – a fair assessment and a right of appeal – because it says they are ‘clearly’ not covered by the agreement. That’s like saying someone doesn’t need a trial because they’re ‘clearly’ guilty.”
She said the Home Office U-turn on jure sanguinis Italian nationals showed it could change its policy when its errors were exposed.

Hawkins said: “This is a simple matter of providing proper due process. Despite our advocacy efforts since early 2025, the Home Office refused to change course, so we have no option but to challenge the policy in court.”

The campaign group is asking the court to declare that the “grant in error policy is unlawful, by breach of the WA and/or common law” and make whatever order is necessary to “excise the offending parts of the published policy”

Many complained that although they were jure sanguinis (direct and unbroken Italian relative), they could not get a passport because the public institutions were in lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic.

Lawyers have also argued that the apparent generosity of the UK, which minimised the evidence required by any EU citizens applying to stay after Brexit, “compounded” the current Home Office policy of removing rights.

The unlawfulness of the policy is compounded by the nature of the EU settlement scheme itself. The UK deliberately implemented a scheme that, in a number of respects, operated more generously than the minimum requirements of the WA.
Hawkins said: “Grants were also made through processes involving evidential flexibility and, in some cases, discretionary decision-making.

“As a result, many status holders cannot know, and are given no means of knowing, whether their status was granted because they satisfied the substantive requirements of the WA, because they satisfied the requirements of Appendix EU as a matter of domestic law, because a caseworker exercised evidential flexibility or discretion in their favour, or because the grant was genuinely erroneous.”

Several cases have come to light of Brazilians who have Italian parents or grandparents. Under Italian law these citizens are Italian by birth but the Home Office alleged they were not because they did not have an Italian passport at the time.
This is not the first time the Home Office has been sued over its implementation of the withdrawal agreement.
In 2022 it was taken to court by the statutory watchdog set up to ensure the Home Office implemented the withdrawal agreement properly.

The Independent Monitoring Authority, backed by the3million, accused the Home Office of putting EU citizens at risk of losing their rights to work or rent a home by forcing them to reapply for settled status once their pre-settled status expired.
High court judges ruled in the IMA’s favour concluding the conditions imposed by the Home Office were unlawful.
A spokesperson for the Home Office said they could not comment as proceedings were ongoing.

articles.title: Remulla: Fake news peddlers want to disrupt institutions, influence courts
articles.summary: Remulla: Fake news peddlers want to disrupt institutions, influence courts

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 5:08pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla slammed fake news peddlers, saying that they only want to "disrupt" institutions.
Remulla previously announced that he wanted to file charges against people who spread disinformation about his illness, despite him being cancer-free since 2023.
Speaking on his radio show at DZRH, Remulla spoke about the possible motivation behind the fake news against him.
“Gusto nila, alugin yung institution… Gusto nila influence yung korte. Kaya contemptuous yun,” Remulla said.
(They want to shake the institution… They want to influence the court. That is why that is contemptuous.)
Remulla had previously commented on former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s supposed security aide, where he disclosed that his office has garnered new enemies as well.
“Ang kalaban ng opisina ko ngayon, marami kaming kalaban na DDS (Diehard Duterte Supporters), at mayroon kaming kalaban na galing din sa… loob, sa hanay ng mga nakasama dati,” Remulla said.
(The enemies of my office now, we have a lot of enemies that are DDS, and now we have enemies from… inside, from the side of our allies before… this is rust, those detractors.)
Remulla said that if he was doing what his enemies were doing, it would be unfair to the people who are accused. He would only say that the evidence would speak for itself.
The Ombudsman said that he would let the Department of Information and Communications Technology handle the matter. —VAL, GMA News

articles.summary: An appearance by Iranian opposition figure Reza Pahlavi is expected to trigger demonstrations in Frankfurt. Meanwhile, Germany's defense minister says he believes military conscription will not be…

blocks.text: Live

An appearance by Iranian opposition figure Reza Pahlavi is expected to trigger demonstrations in Frankfurt. Meanwhile, Germany's defense minister says he believes military conscription will not be needed. DW has more.
Prefer DW on Google

blocks.caption: Reza Pahlavi is the son of the last shah of Iran (FILE: April 2026)Image: John Macdougall/AFP

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Iranian opposition politician Reza Pahlavi is to accept a peace prize in the name of the Iranian people in Frankfurt
Police are preparing for protests and counterprotests by supporters and critics of Pahlavi, with traffic disruption expected
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius says the voluntary recruitment scheme for the German armed forces seems sufficient at present, with no need for conscription

blocks.text: This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 7, and Sunday, November 8, 2026:
November 7, 2026
Frankfurt braces for crowds and disruption at Iran protests
The city of Frankfurt am Main is bracing for another day of protests and traffic disruption on Saturday, with large numbers of Iranians expected to hold protests and counterprotests.

The demonstrations are being prompted by the appearance of exiled Iranian opposition politician Reza Pahlavi, who is to receive a peace prize in the name of Iran's people from the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is affiliated with the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

Pahlavi, the son of Iran's last shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, under whose autocratic rule Iran was governed from 1941 to 1979, was expected to attend a large demonstration in the city's Ostpark and possibly speak there.
Barriers, loudspeaker towers and a stage have already been set up at the park, which is to be the final destination of a march by demonstration participants.
Counterprotests are also expected amid criticism of Pahlavi's presence by Iranian organizations, people held in prison under his father's rule and a number of leftist German parties.
The former German ambassador to the UN, Joachim Rücker, and the erstwhile justice minister, Brigitte Zypries, have also signed an open letter protesting the honor given to Pahlavi.
The last time Pahlavi visited Germany was in April, when he accused Germany and other European countries of standing by while the clerical regime in Iran violently clamped down on protesters.
Frankfurt also saw protests a week ago, with mostly peaceful Gen Z demonstrations calling for better living conditions and education hijacked in the evening by people wanting to loot and vandalize.
Son of Iran's last shah criticizes West on Berlin trip

articles.title: Business groups, civil society orgs back DFA call for sustained PH-China dialogue
articles.summary: Several business, labor, industry, and civil society organizations in the country expressed support Saturday for the Department of Foreign Affairs' (DFA) call for continued dialogue and cooperation…

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 5:07pm

Several business, labor, industry, and civil society organizations in the country expressed support Saturday for the Department of Foreign Affairs' (DFA) call for continued dialogue and cooperation between the Philippines and China.

In a joint statement, the groups commended DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro's recent talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, noting that the engagement reflects the agency's pursuit of principled diplomacy with the country's "top trading partner."

"We recognize the DFA's pragmatic and statesmanlike approach in protecting the country's national interests, particularly its economic development, trade and exports, tourism, overseas Filipino workers, and other vital bilateral engagements with China, the Philippines' largest trading partner," the statement read.

The groups pointed out that amid intensifying global economic competition, the Philippines—much like its ASEAN neighbors—should seek to deepen trade, investment, technology, infrastructure, and tourism ties with Beijing.
They added that while upholding national sovereignty and interests, the country can simultaneously pursue mutually beneficial economic opportunities with China through constructive engagement.

"We therefore support the DFA's pursuit of principled diplomacy and sustained dialogue over confrontation, recognizing that a balanced and constructive relationship with China is essential to advancing Philippine economic security, national interests, and sustainable development," the group added.
The joint statement was signed by the following organizations:
