On Wednesday, Lazaro spoke with Wang Yi, describing their meeting as a "frank and constructive discussion on the direction of Philippines-China relations."
According to Lazaro, both the Philippines and China underscored the need for "continued diplomatic dialogue and proper management of differences anchored on mutual respect." — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: What Ottawa's 'RRSP for life' plan means for Canadian seniors

image.caption: Tax and personal finance experts say that while the new 'RRSP for life' measure in the federal budget would be more convenient, it doesn't address seniors struggling under the rising cost of living. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Business·New
The federal budget proposes a tweak to Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) aimed at simplifying financial planning for thousands of seniors every year.
Experts say the plan cuts complexity, but ignores bigger issues for many Canadian seniors
Canada's new federal budget proposes a tweak to Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) aimed at simplifying financial planning for thousands of seniors every year.
Tax and personal finance experts say while the new "RRSP for life" measure would be more convenient, it does not address seniors who are struggling under rising living costs.

An RRSP is a Canadian savings account that lowers your tax exposure today, and lets your savings and investments grow without being taxed until you retire. They can hold a wide variety of financial assets, including cash, stocks, guaranteed investment certificates (GICs), and exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

For the 2026 tax year, individuals can contribute up to 18 per cent of their earned income in 2025, up to a maximum of $33,810. If you have a workplace pension, the value of those pension contributions is deducted from that 18 per cent limit.
What the federal budget means for your taxes | Hanomansing Live
What are the proposed changes?

Currently, RRSPs must be withdrawn or converted into a Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) when the account holder turns 71. In the new federal budget, Ottawa proposes to allow Canadians to keep their RRSPs after they reach that age.
Currently, if someone dies after age 71 with a RRIF, the account can be transferred to a spouse without closing it or triggering tax paperwork. That's not the case today with RRSPs.

Ottawa's budget proposal would "allow a surviving spouse or partner to become a successor holder of an RRSP, and simplify tax-free transfers to qualified survivors after the death of the account holder."
A public consultation on the plan started on Thursday, and will run until Jan. 8, 2027.

items: 7 takeaways from the Carney government's 2nd budget
Carney's new budget aims to end homelessness in 10 years

blocks.text: Jamie Golombek, managing director, tax and estate planning at CIBC Private Wealth Management, says today most 71-year-olds choose to convert their RRSPs to RRIFs to avoid the tax applied if they choose to cash out.
"It's a complex administrative thing for hundreds of thousands at least every year," he told CBC News.
"What the government is saying is, 'Why not have an RRSP for life?' In other words, an RRSP that you basically have until the day you die."

Under the proposed change, the government would require RRSP holders to withdraw a minimum percentage of their savings each year, starting at age 72. These percentages are based on average life expectancy to ensure that retirement savings is paid out and taxed gradually for the rest of the owner's lifetime.
John Fragos, press secretary to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, confirmed to CBC News that under the government's proposal, RRSP account holders cannot contribute after age 71.
Budget 2026: Carney makes 'big bet' for investment, opposition blasts affordability moves
Why do the changes matter?

Aaron Hector, senior wealth advisor at Calgary-based Tier Wealth says simplifying the financial landscape for seniors is a smart move by the government. He also praises the proposal to allow RRSPs to be easily transferred after death.

"Not needing someone to go through the paperwork process of converting an RRSP into a RRIF just makes a lot of common sense for me," he said. "Heaven forbid it slips through the cracks. It could create some issues for people."

Li Zhang, director of social impact at Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada, sees the government's "RRSP for life" proposal as "more of a nomenclature change," that ignores bigger issues for seniors.
Firstly, she estimates only 33 to 37 per cent of Canadians actually have access to a pension.

"You're not actually talking about a lot of people who have a lot of retirement savings assets," she said. "If you've walked by food banks, and you look at the line, it's the really young or the really old."

items: From groceries to tax credits, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?

blocks.text: She says another problem for RRSP holders is that the mandatory withdrawals can make it difficult to balance their income. "That then triggers higher levels of taxation," she said.
While the consultation period for this plan runs until Jan. 8, Golombek expects it could take much longer to enact these changes if Ottawa elects to make them.
"I think it's going to be a few years before we see the ultimate merger of these, or at least the elimination of the RRIF."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: A powerful veterinary sedative is being added to street fentanyl — and ERs are struggling to cope
articles.summary: Emergency physicians across Canada say a powerful veterinary sedative is being added to fentanyl sold on streets, complicating their response to overdoses as they juggle patients.

image.caption: A person is brought into the emergency room of Toronto General Hospital in 2022. Emergency physicians across Canada say a powerful veterinary sedative is being added to fentanyl sold on streets, complicating their response to overdoses as they juggle patients. (Carlos Osorio/CBC)

blocks.text: Emergency physicians across Canada say a powerful veterinary sedative is being added to fentanyl sold on streets, complicating their response to overdoses as they juggle patients.

Medetomidine, a synthetic sedative, is used in veterinary surgery and has not been approved for use in humans, nor have its effects on people been well studied. The effect of fentanyl, a key driver of the opioid epidemic in this country, lasts half as long as that of heroin; adulterants like medetomidine are taken to extend it.

The synthetic was first detected in 2023 in Quebec, B.C. and Ontario, with detections increasing substantially in the latter two provinces since then, according to a report from the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA). It has also been found in the Maritime region, and Saskatchewan and Yukon have seen sharp increases this year.

This fall, researchers in Philadelphia, where the additive has become common, flagged that physicians were reporting a "novel withdrawal syndrome" among those with opioid use disorder living in areas with a high level of medetomidine in the drug supply. Symptoms of the condition, which can develop quickly, include a severely elevated heartbeat, vomiting, hypertension, agitated delirium and even reports of organ damage.

Now, Canadian overdose prevention workers and emergency physicians are struggling to deal with it, too. They also report difficulties in treating medetomidine withdrawal, which can lead to complications like heart attacks or strokes from the blood pressure, said Dr. Monty Ghosh, a Calgary-based addictions physician and researcher.
"These are the things that we kind of have to match that we didn't have to match before," Ghosh said. "It's sort of skewed our management strategies for these individuals."
Overdose deaths remain 'unacceptably high' despite 2025 decrease, Canada's top doctor says
Drowsy patients coupled with heart attack risks

Taking opioids can make it difficult for a person to breathe. Add in medetomidine, said Ghosh, and they'll also become much drowsier, with low blood pressure and a low heart rate that can stay down for long periods of time.
"It can be very dangerous," he said, because that reduces blood flow to vital organs, which can lead to serious complications, as well as slow breathing.

At overdose prevention sites in B.C. and Montreal, nurses also say they're concerned about users having very low heart rates and becoming dizzy and unresponsive for hours, according to a CCSA presentation. Regularly monitoring a person's pulse, heart rate and oxygen levels now matters more, because these changes can be delayed compared with previous drugs and adulterants.

When reversing an overdose where medetomidine is involved, Substance Use Philly noted it is important to focus on the person's breathing rather than their responsiveness, given that medetomidine is a sedative and therefore does not respond to naloxone, which reverses opioid overdoses.
Medetomidine withdrawal, meanwhile, can come on quickly and brings its own set of problems, like the question of how much vomiting is too much.

Dr. Sahil Gupta, who works in Toronto, says patients experiencing medetomidine withdrawal require hospitalization or intensive care medications because breathing and consciousness need to be monitored for a longer period of time than with opioid withdrawal.
"In our emergency departments, [these] patients take a longer amount of time, both from a nursing, staff physician and time within the hospitals" perspective.

items: Opioid deaths dropped 23% in 2025 — bringing 'cautious optimism' from Canada's top doctor

blocks.text: While the goal is to support breathing to prevent the brain from starving of oxygen, in extreme circumstances, patients will need to be put on a ventilator, he said.

A box of Narcan sits at a community outreach storefront in Philadelphia in 2023. Generically known as naloxone, the medication used revive people who have stopped breathing doesn’t reverse the effects if opioids are absent. (Matt Rourke/The Associated Press)

"[Resource] strains like this tend to actually create a lot of disruption and cause increased wait times, overcrowding," Gupta said. "Often the patients experiencing the medetomidine withdrawal are requiring hospitalization or intensive care meds, as well, which are much more high-resource areas."
Gupta said unless the whole continuum of homelessness and socioeconomic factors are addressed, "we're really not going to make inroads."
Proposed solutions
One doctor in Alberta helped create a program meant to try and address emergency room overcrowding.

The Edmonton program, called Bridge Healing, looks to address homelessness among those making repeat hospital visits, said Dr. Louis Hugo Francescutti, a professor in the School of Public Health at the University of Alberta who works as an emergency physician.

If someone comes to the emergency department with no fixed address, Francescutti said they're asked two questions: whether they are homeless, and whether they want a chance to get their life together again.

items: What Canada's wastewater reveals about drug use in 8 cities
Province says consumption site improving safety, but some businesses disagree

blocks.text: "If they say yes and there's beds available, we send them by cab to these purpose-built buildings, where we provide them free-of-charge accommodation," he said, along with services including access to a medical clinic to start to address their needs.
"Emergency department staff are becoming morally distressed," he said. "They're burning out because they see a problem that is solvable if we had the right people intervening."
He said that includes better access to specialized clinics and practitioners like social workers.
Many homeless people return to the ER after being discharged. This program hopes to change that

However, some practitioners say there is another missing element: safe consumption sites, many of which were closed down in provinces like Ontario, with the provincial government saying the sites encouraged drug use.

items: Toronto hospital to greatly expand permanent housing program that reduces ER visits

blocks.text: At these sites, workers would be able to assess comatose overdose patients, potentially giving them oxygen or a small dose of naloxone so they can avoid being put into full opioid withdrawal, said Dr. Raghu Venugopal, an emergency physician at three downtown Toronto hospitals.
"This really matters because if you want safe subways, if you want safe parks, if you want a better-functioning ER, there is a place for people who need to use drugs," he said.

Indeed, without the supervised sites, people who previously would have been revived at the sites now need to go to emergency, a 2026 report by Gillian Kolla of Memorial University's medicine faculty and epidemiologist Tara Gomes of the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network suggests, delaying care for other life-threatening conditions such as heart attacks and traumatic injuries from vehicle collisions.
Asked to respond to the emergency physicians' calls, Ontario's Health Ministry pointed to its approach.

"Instead of giving people tools to use harmful, illegal drugs, our government is helping people break the tragic cycle of drug addiction by making record investments in more mental health and wraparound supports," Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario's health minister, said in an email.

"Across the province, we are investing a historic $560 million to build 29 Homeless and Addictions Recovery Treatment (HART) Hubs, including 4 in Toronto, replacing the failed approach of drug injection sites."
Barnes said Ontario's 29 HART hubs are open to set people on a path to recovery, with each hub receiving four times more funding than the drug sites.

articles.title: Tax relief could be coming for Canadian artists — but how does it work?
articles.summary: The newly proposed Canada Creative Credit tax relief is supposed to help artists. But how much can artists really expect in their pockets? Which kind of artists can benefit from it? And when — if…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne arrive in the House of Commons to table the federal budget on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: If you're a Canadian artist who followed Thursday's federal budget release, you might believe you're getting a windfall.

"In Budget 2026, we’re backing the Canadian artists who tell our stories," Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X, shortly after Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne made a similar announcement in the House of Commons, revealing the Canada Creative Credit.
This tax credit is aimed specifically at those earning their income from "original and creative artistic works" in the country, according to the budget.
"That means if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to $45,000 of income derived from your creative work," Carney added in his post.
But how much can artists really expect in their pockets? Which kind of artists can even benefit from this? And when — if ever — is this actually taking effect?
What the latest federal budget means for national museums in Ottawa
What is the Canada Creative Credit?

The budget says it will likely take the form of a non-refundable tax credit that would "provide tax recognition on up to $45,000 of annual qualifying net business income derived from original and creative artistic works."
A non-refundable tax credit is a set reduction in the amount of income tax someone owes at the end of the year, says Chris Raymond, a tax consultant and content creator.
In short, the government decides your total income tax based on your income. The credit is then subtracted from that amount to reduce your total taxes owed.

What makes credits like the Canada Creative Credit "non-refundable" is that they cannot reduce that amount below zero. If the credit is bigger than your taxes, you don't get to cash out the remainder as a refund.
"The taxable income is the number that we actually calculate how much tax you owe on," Raymond said. "Once that tax number is calculated, that's where the non-refundable credits come into play."
How much money could you get?
Canadians are already covered by a non-refundable tax credit called the Basic Personal Amount, which applies to roughly $16,000 for most incomes.

The Canada Creative Credit would likely cover the difference between the Basic Personal Amount and the government's goal of $45,000, says Robert Gillezeau, an assistant professor of economic analysis and policy at the University of Toronto.

"If you're an artist making whatever, $40,000, $50,000, all the way up to $100,000, this is going to be a meaningful shift in what your income looks like at the end of the day," he said, adding that it could amount to several thousand dollars annually for those eligible.
"It should be a large enough incentive that it will cause some people to work in this area who would otherwise work somewhere else."

items: Carney’s big federal budget bets
Your questions about this year's federal budget, answered

blocks.text: However, that ignores a potentially large additional source of tax, said Toronto-based chartered professional accountant (CPA) and content creator Mohammed Al-khooly.
"If someone wants to truly be exempt on the first $45,000 income, then the provinces would also have to propose a similar credit for the provincial taxes," Al-khooly said.
"It's not necessarily tax-free. It's tax-free for just federal purposes."
Who would be eligible?
This is where things get tricky.
CPA Sam Cao pointed out that the budget says the government will support young Canadian artists and "Canadian painters, sculptors, ceramicists, writers, musicians, actors are our storytellers."

But there is "no exact definition" within the budget that specifies which types of artists would be eligible. So there's little to no way to know whether, for example, a violin teacher or a filmmaker is more likely to be approved.
"They're going to have some type of prescriptive list that demarcates a bunch of workers being in, and other workers being out. It's going to be arbitrary in some ways," Gillezeau said.

"They talk about supporting creativity and the arts broadly; like, any type of writing could fall within that. And if, you know … any type of original writing is going to be eligible, the cost of this credit will just absolutely balloon."

When asked whether there was any firm definition of which artists would qualify, a Department of Finance official referred CBC News to the budget release. It said further details will be announced in the spring economic update in 2027.
Printed copies of the 2026 federal budget. (David Thurton/ CBC)
How likely is it to happen?
Far less than a confirmed payday, Raymond said, the Canada Creative Credit is more the proposition of a plan.

"Obviously the budget hasn't been passed. But they haven't said that if the budget is passed, that this is coming into play," he said. "What they have said is that they have an idea and a concept of how this would work. They're going to consult with people in the industry about it."

There are other targeted tax credits in Canada, such as for teachers and volunteer firefighters. Still, Cao said, if the Canada Creative Credit took a form even somewhat similar to how it is currently described, it would be a unique step.
"This is probably the first tax credit of its kind that specifically targets self-employed individuals through a non-refundable personal income tax credit," he said.
LISTEN | The federal budget explained:
The Current20:14Breaking down the federal budget

Gillezeau noted tax policies targeted at specific professions are typically disliked by economists, comparing the Canada Creative Credit's possible end-status to the "boutique" tax credits of the Stephen Harper era that ballooned the tax code to absurd lengths.
There are also similarities to subsidies for the arts seen in the New Deal of the 1930s, in which the U.S. government subsidized works of art for the public good.
What is different here is the proposal of large, profession-targeted tax credits for income, Gillezeau said. Though what it looks like should it come to fruition is still almost entirely a mystery.
"It's enough to think about [whether] it is a valuable piece of public policy or not," he said. "But the actual implementation details certainly are nowhere close to being there."

articles.title: Canada's military is using Palantir software. What are the risks?
articles.summary: Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with U.S. tech firm Palantir. Experts warn the deals could expose military data to U.S. authorities and deepen Canada's reliance on foreign technology, while…

blocks.text: Why Canada’s military deal with Palantir sparks sovereignty fears

Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with Palantir, a controversial U.S. software company. Experts warn the deals could expose Canadian military data to U.S. authorities and leave Canada reliant on critical technology supplied by a foreign company.

Documents obtained by the Investigative Journalism Foundation revealed that the Department of National Defence (DND) has had a contract for Palantir's Gotham software since 2020 that was internally flagged as "not for public disclosure." Initially valued at $14 million, it could be worth up to $63 million.

DND told CBC News that Gotham brings together information from military databases and operates on closed, classified networks inside secure facilities in Canada. The department declined to say exactly what information Gotham processes, citing national-security concerns.
DND says its security assessment determined that no government data, prompts, outputs or metadata handled under the contracts could be stored, accessed or processed outside Canada.

But experts argue U.S. law could still provide American authorities with a means to acquire information within an American company's possession, custody or control. Others warn Canada could become dependent on military technology that would be difficult to replace.
A view of the Palantir building is seen during the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2026 in Davos, Switzerland, in January. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)
Why is Palantir controversial?
Palantir Technologies was co-founded in 2003 by five people, including CEO Alex Karp and board chair Peter Thiel. It has since become a major technology contractor for governments and militaries.
Its software integrates information from multiple datasets so users can identify connections and patterns across large amounts of information.

Michael Steinberger, a journalist and author of The Philosopher in the Valley: Alex Karp, Palantir, and the Rise of the Surveillance State, said the company has drawn criticism over its involvement in military operations and immigration enforcement in the United States.
Some of its most important work, he said, involves Project Maven, the U.S. military's artificial-intelligence program used to analyze military data and support targeting operations.
"This is being used extensively now in U.S. military actions," Steinberger said.

When asked about Project Maven, a Palantir spokesperson told CBC News: "We do not conduct surveillance. The Maven platform provides the U.S. warfighter a live, synchronized view of the battlespace to help them make better-informed decisions and reduce errors … all of this is conducted with strong safeguards and accountability logs."
Palantir's work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also drawn criticism.
"Its technology seems to be a critical node in the immigration crackdown that's happening here in the United States right now," Steinberger said.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp is shown at the 48th Annual Meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos in 2018. (Peter Klaunzer/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock)
The company has also increasingly identified itself with U.S. national interests.
U.S. President Donald Trump praised Palantir earlier this year for having "great war-fighting capabilities and equipment."

In June, Palantir posted on X a list of 22 principles drawn from The Technological Republic, a book co-written by Karp. They include the assertion that Silicon Valley has an "obligation to participate in the defense of the nation" and describe some cultures as "dysfunctional and regressive."
Karp has also appeared in company advertising saying "the West is superior, and we have to fight for these values."

Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, an independent public policy think tank, said the concern extends beyond Palantir's politics to Canada's reliance on an outside supplier for critical digital infrastructure.
"We're potentially growing a digital dependency, enriching what is fundamentally a U.S. company at the expense of our sovereignty," she said.

A protester opposed to data analytics firm Palantir Technologies' role in the National Health Service (NHS) holds a sign in a demonstration outside St Thomas' Hospital during a global day of action against the company's healthcare contracts, in London, in October. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)
Other countries becoming less reliant
The debate over Palantir comes amid a broader push in Europe for "digital sovereignty" — greater domestic control over technology and data.
In July, France and Germany pledged to reduce reliance on foreign providers by examining domestic alternatives after ending Palantir's contracts with their intelligence services.

In the U.K., MPs have called on the government to end Palantir's 330-million-pound ($619 million Cdn) National Health Service contract, citing "serious mistrust" of the company after a Financial Times report that a small number of company employees had access to identifiable patient data in the Palantir-built platform. The National Data Guardian, an independent adviser on the use of health and social-care data in England, said the incident breached data-governance principles.

A Palantir spokesperson at the time told the Financial Times that "Palantir software can only be used to process data precisely in line with the instruction of the customer. Using the data for anything else would not only be illegal but technically impossible due to granular access controls overseen by the NHS."
Barry Appleton, an international lawyer who practises both Canadian and American law, says the U.S. CLOUD Act could compel U.S. companies to produce data stored outside the United States. (CBC)
Should Canada be concerned?
One potential concern is whether U.S. authorities could compel access to Canadian information.

Barry Appleton, an international lawyer who practises both Canadian and American law, pointed to the U.S. CLOUD Act, which allows authorities, with appropriate legal process, to compel covered U.S. companies to produce data within their possession, custody or control, regardless of whether it is stored inside or outside the United States.
"I'm talking to you today while we're having massive trade wars," Appleton said. "Do I want Canada's trade strategy to be able to be surveilled and read by the United States today? No, I don't."

DND says its Palantir systems have been assessed for this kind of exposure. It says government data, prompts, outputs or metadata could not be stored, accessed or processed outside Canada and that Gotham information is protected on closed, classified networks in secure Canadian facilities.
"The United States CLOUD Act does not have any authority over servers located in Canada," DND said.
Appleton disputes that interpretation.
"The CLOUD Act is not about where the server is located," he said.

"Any data at any time that Palantir has, if it was subject to an order under the CLOUD Act would have to be produced," Appleton said because "it's decided by American courts under American law, not under Canadian law."

Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a reception with business leaders, at the 56th annual World Economic Forum (WEF), in Davos, in January 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Jennifer Evans, a policy researcher and founder of PatternPulse AI, said DND's statement that data is stored on closed, classified networks in Canada doesn't make clear what level of security is being used.
She agreed with Appleton that the CLOUD Act "means that there is potential data visibility to some of the highest levels in the U.S. government."
Evans said DND should disclose more about its contract with Palantir, including whether it uses air-gapping, which isolates computers or networks from unsecured networks and the internet.
A Palantir spokesperson told CBC News in an email that it is "a software company" and rejected suggestions that the company takes ownership of or uses its customers' information.
"Our customers own and control their own data. Palantir never uses or retains customer data for its own purposes or shares data with other customers," the spokesperson told CBC News.
A second potential risk is Canada's dependence on a foreign supplier for military technology.

A Ukrainian artilleryman sets up a Starlink satellite internet system near the front line in the Donetsk region in October 2026. Ukrainian officials said Starlink speeds had been throttled earlier that month, disrupting military operations. (Stringer/File Photo/Reuters)

Bednar points to Space X's Starlink internet technology, owned by Elon Musk. Beginning Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink's speeds, disrupting military activity. The accusations came after Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply the world with millions of tonnes of Russian diesel.
While it's unclear who was responsible for the slowdown, Bednar says the episode shows how reliance on a company with ties to the U.S. government can leave militaries vulnerable.
"These are not neutral technologies. So let's stop treating them as if they're neutral," Bednar said.
Canadian alternatives?
Evans said few companies compete with the breadth of Palantir's software but pointed to Canadian alternatives, including Vancouver-based Caseway and Ottawa-based Anvil.
"They don't come anywhere close to the breadth and depth that Palantir offers," she said. She added that it will take time for them to develop comparable technology.
Bednar said Canada should nevertheless invest in developing that technology domestically.
"Building and owning this kind of necessary digital infrastructure for defence should be a primary goal for Canada," she said.

articles.title: Sewing is having a moment. Here’s why
articles.summary: Sewing hobbyists and the people who teach them say a number of factors — including renewed interest in analog hobbies and growing concern about the impacts of fast fashion — are driving more…

image.caption: A renewed interest in non-digital hobbies and growing concern about the impacts of fast fashion are driving more Canadians to learn how to sew. (Jordi Calvera/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: The Current·New

Sewing hobbyists and the people who teach them say a number of factors — including renewed interest in analog hobbies and growing concern about the impacts of fast fashion — are driving more Canadians to pick up a needle and thread.
Increased interest in sustainable fashion and analog hobbies are driving some Canadians to learn to sew
LISTEN | The common threads in sewing culture today:
The Current22:42Sewing is back!
Depending on the corner of the internet you inhabit, you may have noticed that the feeds are full of sewing enthusiasts.
Look up "thrift flips" on Instagram or TikTok and you'll find creators remaking second-hand garments into new ones, or old quilts into hoodies and track suits.

On Pinterest, searches for "sewing ideas" are up 118 per cent year over year by its Canadian users, while those for "beginner sewing projects" rose 67 per cent, according to data provided to CBC News by the platform.

"A generation raised on fast fashion is rediscovering the value of making and repairing their own clothes," said Sabine Weber, a professor of fashion at Seneca Polytechnic College in Toronto whose PhD research focused on sustainable fashion.
"And now they have discovered thrifting."

Referencing data from Trendex North America, a Canadian apparel market intelligence firm, Weber says the clothing resale market was forecast to grow from around $3.8 billion in 2022 to almost $6 billion in 2026.
Students from Seneca Polytechnic on a visit to the Textile Museum of Canada in Toronto. (Submitted by Sabine Weber)
That shift in shopping habits has prompted people to learn how to make small repairs to thrifted finds, and from there to try more ambitious upcycling projects, she says.
"And then you want to really … show your individuality and your self-expression by making your own clothes."

In Victoria, Erin Kerr says she began in earnest to develop her sewing skills a few years ago. "I had a scrunchie brand called Hair of the Dog that ended up doing pretty well … but I was just kind of sewing rectangles over and over," Kerr told The Current.
Once she expanded her repertoire, Kerr began to offer sewing lessons to get more out of her studio space and bring in a little extra cash.
"We immediately had an email list of hundreds of people that were interested in learning to sew from us," she said.
What started as a weekend project has since morphed into the Sewing Club, a specialty shop and school that offers patterns, fabric, tools and a range of sewing workshops.

"There's definitely a lot of people that want to take their time with sewing and are into the whole kind of slow fashion movement," said Kerr. Others want to learn to alter clothes that don't fit well off the rack, or start from scratch and make something new.
Embracing the analog
There's also the offline nature of the craft, says Weber.
"It's a very big contrast to all the typing we do and all the machines and phones and iPads and whatever."

Branislava Pavlovic started sewing in spring 2025 and one of her most prized projects is this jumpsuit made of vintage Toronto Blue Jays bedsheets, which she wears to games. (Submitted by Branislava Pavlovic)
As Branislava Pavlovic points out, "it's literally impossible to be on your phone and sew at the same time."
She took up sewing in the spring of 2025 with beginner classes at the Neon Needle in Toronto and now works there as studio manager and instructor.

"We find that there's a lot of people who are in tech jobs, engineers and administrators, that just want to come and just do nothing like what they do all day, but actually do something for themselves and be creative."

Candice Alvarez, who sews and designs patterns from her home studio in Burlington, Ont., says she thinks the increased interest coincides with a shift in people's understanding of the impacts of fast fashion. (Amanda Grant/CBC)
Ishmam Sarker says he was inspired by some of the sewing content he was seeing on Instagram and TikTok.
"I've always been into fashion … And then I guess the algorithm worked in my favour. It slowly started to push some sewing-specific content on it," Sarker said.
He followed a tutorial on how to make a tote bag and took on more ambitious projects from there.
"I started just getting patterns from Fabricland and a bunch of other places online as well," he told The Current at a fabric swap in Toronto.
YouTube, he said, "helps a lot."
Candice Alvarez says she thinks social media has pushed hobbies like this to the forefront.
"And I think that's incredible because honestly, I had no idea that people were sewing their own clothes before I started," she said.
Alvarez, who now sews and designs patterns from her home studio in Burlington, Ont., says she also thinks the increased interest coincides with a shift in the way people look at fashion.
"Like fast fashion — for a while, people loved it," she said. "You could buy a T-shirt for $10 and it was amazing."
Whereas "people now, their eyes are opened to the fashion industry and how damaging it can be to the environment, and the labour [conditions] and like all of it."
Getting started
Those who are thinking of taking up sewing can check out an endless supply of tutorials online.
But brick-and-mortar studios where people can take in-person classes seem to be increasing in number.
The Neon Needle in Toronto is a sewing studio that offers a range of sewing classes and workshops. (Submitted by The Neon Needle)

For example, in Toronto, the Neon Needle transitioned fully from tailor shop to sewing-lesson studio in February 2024. Downtown Sewing opened in April 2025 and SewBar, a combined sewing studio and coffee shop is set to open soon.
Hey Soft Spot opened in Vancouver in September, Calgary's Sew Happy in August and Winnipeg's Lilax Studio in April.
Back in Victoria, at the Sewing Club, Kerr recommends keeping expectations modest at the start.

"I would say don't get too emotionally attached to your first project because it's probably going to look bad," she said. "So don't focus too much on the outcome. It's more the process and building your skills."
Produced by Amanda Grant

articles.title: Problematic or protected? The debate over filming police in real time
articles.summary: Social media posts showing real-time positions of police officers in a standoff with an armed suspect at the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus on Monday night prompted a stern warning from…

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Social media posts showing real-time positions of police officers in a standoff with an armed suspect at the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus on Monday night prompted a stern warning from police, but legal experts say the law isn't clear-cut on the issue.
Police say posting real-time positions a 'blatant safety concern,' but experts say law murky
Posting officer positions is 'problematic,' but is it actually illegal?

"We saw many members of the public uploading images of the position of police officers during this active incident," Peel Regional Police Const. Tyler Bell said at a news conference on Tuesday. "This is a blatant safety concern. Doing so puts our officers in harm's way and any potential victims or hostages inside."

"Canadians have the right that is constitutionally protected to film on-duty police officers, but that right ends the second it interferes with the police operation or compromises the safety of people involved."

The comments followed a lengthy standoff between officers and a 19-year-old man who allegedly barricaded himself with a weapon inside a residential unit the university's McLuhan Court residence. The school issued a shelter-in-place order for students in the area that was later lifted after police said the man was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

items: Man dead, SIU investigating after incident at U of T Mississauga: police

blocks.text: Bell said photos and videos of officers in their tactical positions, with weapons pointed toward the buildings were circulating on social media as the incident was evolving. While people are allowed to film police in public settings, he said doing so during an active incident can can jeopardize investigations.

"The act of filming isn't the issue. It's the putting it out so everybody can see it, including bad actors. Giving up the position of an officer can compromise their safety or the safety other others. It's a no-no," Bell said in an interview with CBC News.
"By all means, film it and post it afterwards when the situation safe."
What does the law say?
However, some legal experts say whether the practice is actually illegal is a grey area.

While it is generally legal to film the police in public settings, it can become a problem if it interferes with officers doing their job, said Howard Sapers, executive director of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA).
Examples include physically obstructing the police or filming evidence, which could result in a phone being seized.

items: Toronto police can't stop you from filming them, nor seize your phone, lawyer says

blocks.text: "The police could advise and say 'We wish you wouldn't do that,' but that's very different from them ordering you not to do it," said Sapers.

"And if they do order you not to do it, the general advice is to comply because that could or could not be a lawful request or a lawful demand. That would be something that could be tested in court, but if you refuse to comply, the refusal becomes an offence."

Sapers says in those instances, people should seek clarity from police on why they're asking them not to record. In the case of Monday's incident, there was no explicit legal order to not film and share.

Police officers and the SIU outside of a student residence at the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus on Nov. 2, 2026. Officers were involved in a lengthy standoff after a 19-year-old man allegedly barricaded himself inside a residential unit with a weapon. (Jacob Estrin/CBC)

Posting in real-time can fall under the umbrella of obstructing a police officer, which is a criminal offence under Section 129 of the Criminal Code, said Howard Morton, a former Special Investigations Unit director and criminal defence lawyer.
But in order for someone to be found guilty, "wilful intention" must be proven, he said.
"You would have to intentionally, with a specific intent, interfere with an investigation — either by jeopardizing an officer or just letting the bad guys know what the police are doing," he said.
"You could interfere by streaming [incidents] live."
Students say social media kept them in the loop

Some students CBC News spoke to, said although they were receiving regular updates with safety instructions from police and UTM campus officials, Instagram and Reddit allowed them to share information and learn why there was a lockdown in the first place.

"I saw one [person] from a window who I think was videoing the police, some other posts were just rumours of what could have possibly happened because when it first happened, no one knew what was going on," said second-year student Efe Otomewo.
"Some people were saying fire, some people were saying shooting, some people saying fireworks were being set off. So that was mostly the way that we got our information."
There was a large police presence in the area of Mississauga Road and Outer Circle Road, at the University of Toronto Mississauga campus, on Monday night. (Zachary Proulx/CBC)
Many students said they didn't share the videos because residence leaders told them not to and they didn't want to add to online rumours.

"More details would've been more helpful but I understand that they can't really give the full rundown to not cause so much panic," said first-year student Beulah Karibo. "But it still creates a panic if people hear there's a lockdown and a shooting.
Meanwhile, Bell said he understands the curiosity but explained police were releasing information on a need-to-know basis, adding that resolving the incident safely was their top priority.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Isha Bhargava is a multiplatform reporter for CBC News in Peel Region where she covers everything from local news to current affairs and human interest stories. She was previously with CBC London. You can reach out to her with your story ideas at isha.bhargava@cbc.ca
With files from Gaurav Bhatt

articles.title: Northern, remote RCMP detachments chronically and critically understaffed: internal report
articles.summary: Northern and isolated RCMP detachments have become "chronically and at times critically" understaffed, according to an internal evaluation report — the latest document pointing to retention and…

image.caption: An RCMP officer and his work dog take a walk in Frobisher Bay in Iqaluit, Nunavut, in 2019. An internal report flags several issues making it difficult for the national police force to staff its most remote outposts. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Northern and isolated RCMP detachments have become "chronically and at times critically" understaffed, according to an internal evaluation report — the latest document pointing to retention and recruitment issues within the storied organization.
Participants flagged family-related issues, high cost of living as deterrents

The June 2026 evaluation, made public last month, found Mounties' interest in staffing northern and isolated posts is limited and the RMCP's recruitment practices are not aligned with the staffing needs in these detachments.

"Northern and isolated posts face a complex set of barriers that significantly hinder recruitment, retention and overall staffing stability. A central challenge is isolation, both physical and organizational," said the report.
Several divisions report critical shortages in their northern and isolated posts.

Hard vacancy rates, where positions are open due to things like retirements, resignations or permanent transfers, were over 20 per cent in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut during the third quarter of this fiscal year. Manitoba's vacancy rate hovered just below 20 per cent, while Saskatchewan reported nearly 15 per cent.

items: Premiers tell Ottawa they 'urgently' want negotiations to begin on future of the RCMP
RCMP failed to recruit enough officers to meet operational needs: auditor general

blocks.text: "A critical theme identified in participant feedback was the cumulative impact of operational pressures, isolation and the severity of violence in some posts on mental health," said the report.
Women, racialized members and those with adult dependents who took part in the RCMP's review rated a feeling of isolation as a barrier higher and more often than other groups.
The report also noted a generational shift "with younger members placing greater emphasis on proximity to family and work-life balance than on traditional notions of duty."
Testifying before a parliamentary committee earlier this fall, RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said that's changed in his decades with the organization.

"When I went through training, a lot of people were seeking a northern adventure — and it was an adventure. It's a good way to be embedded in community policing. It's completely different policing," he said.
"When people have to mobilize a family, or if they're divorced and have shared custody, it's a challenge sometimes to get people up to the North."
Limited success in past efforts

The RCMP has tried to bring in strategies to confront some of those issues with limited success, according to the report. One program gave members their preferred division in exchange for first accepting a posting to a less desirable location. However the report raised concerns about the RCMP approving more postings than they could accommodate.

Historically the RCMP would assign cadets to their first post after completing their training. In 2023, it brought in a plan that allowed new applicants to choose their division. While that successfully increased the number of applicants, it resulted "in divisions in need receiving less cadets, thus compounding existing staffing challenges."

The report said that recruiting for policing careers has become increasingly challenging across Canada, not just for the RCMP. But it noted that competitive environment can make it harder for the force to attract candidates who don't want to move.
"Despite these strategies and incentives, northern and remote detachments are chronically, and at times critically, understaffed," according to the evaluation.
RCMP staffing should be Arctic security issue: author

Kent Roach, author of the book Red Alert: The Future of the RCMP, said as the federal government looks to shore up Arctic security it needs to consider the long-term viability of the RCMP as the police of jurisdiction in the North.

"It seems to me that we're spending billions on Arctic security, national security, while there are some real problems with community security and community safety in the Far North," the University of Toronto professor said.
"You cannot have national security and national sovereignty in the North without doing the basics of community safety."

Retention and recruitment issues are RCMP-wide. An auditor general report earlier this year said the RCMP had not recruited enough new officers or effectively assigned its members to meet its operational needs "which could make it more challenging for the force to prevent and investigate crime, maintain peace and order and contribute to national security."

In his book, Roach argues it's not feasible for the RCMP to continue to split its mandate between the front-line policing it does in eight provinces and the three territories and its federal policing mandate leading investigations into terrorism, espionage and organized crime.
‘I want us to grow in numbers:’ New RCMP commissioner discusses his top priority for the organization
Despite calls for transformation, Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has said it will keep the RCMP's dual mandate.
"I am not terribly optimistic about how we're going to pull out of this downward spiral," said Roach.

The report recommended developing a co-ordinated strategy to address northern staffing needs and calls on the RCMP brass to explore opportunities to increase targeted recruitment efforts to attract applicants who best meet the requirement in these posts.
It also calls on leadership to review and modernize incentives to help the organization attract and retain members in northern and isolated locations.
According to the report, the RCMP has reviewed and accepted the findings and recommendations.

articles.title: MLB teams face tough calls on signings, trades as current labour deal runs out
articles.summary: Major League Baseball teams have tough calls to make this month, as they scramble to get the players they want on their rosters during an off-season that may be truncated amid contentious labour…

image.caption: Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred is seen speaking to members of the media in Milwaukee last month. The league's owners are pushing to establish a salary cap in their sport, against strong opposition from pro baseball players. (Ashley Landis/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: MLB

Major League Baseball teams have tough calls to make this month, as they scramble to get the players they want on their rosters during an off-season that may be truncated amid contentious labour negotiations.
Off-season could be shortened if lockout occurs, as owners push for salary cap

MLB's collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, at which point a lockout is widely expected. That's because team owners are pushing to change the economic system of their game to limit how much teams can spend on their payrolls. This has received strong opposition from the players.
The two sides appear dug in. They've each amassed large war chests and MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has admitted concern that a long work stoppage could be coming.
For now, the league's 30 teams have the rest of November to get their organizations set up for next season, while the existing agreement winds down.

Bruce Meyer, the interim executive director of the Major League Baseball Players Association, has described the owners' push for a salary cap as a 'nuclear bomb' that will make labour negotiations much more difficult. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)
While organizations will have done their homework on what the next labour agreement could bring, no one knows what the final deal will be until it is reached.

Observers with front office experience say that teams navigating this moment will have to weigh their need to get better against the risk that contracts signed today could carry unforeseen consequences tomorrow.
Dan Duquette, a former baseball executive with three MLB franchises, expects teams may have to temper their spending plans to some extent, given the uncertainty.
"I think teams are going to tighten their belts and take a look at what their critical investments are for next season," he said in an interview with CBC News.

Tim Purpura, left, reacts to being doused with champagne by Houston Astros infielder Adam Everett on Oct. 2, 2005, the day the club clinched a wild card spot on the last day of the regular season. The Astros went to the World Series that year, with Purpura as team's general manager. (Richard Carson/Reuters)
Fellow former MLB executive Tim Purpura says teams will nonetheless be on the lookout for ways to improve their rosters, whether or not a new labour agreement is on the horizon.

"You've got to strike while the iron's hot and get in there," said Purpura, whose career in baseball included serving as the general manager of the Houston Astros for several seasons, including in 2005, when the team went to the World Series.
Preparing for the unknown
While there's no guarantee the team owners will get a salary cap enacted, the league's teams will still weigh the implications of a potential cap coming forward.
Purpura says it's the norm that teams have to prepare for a variety of scenarios when the off-season arrives, including labour shortages.

"When we were in those situations, we were constantly doing financial models to see, 'OK, if they change this rule, this is going to affect us in this way,'" said Purpura, who was working in baseball during the 1994 season in which a strike — also over a proposed salary cap — wiped out the World Series.
The owners threw MLB teams a change-up of sorts this week, when they suggested that a cap could be delayed until 2028, backing down from an earlier call to have a cap in 2027.

Milwaukee Brewers catcher William Contreras, the MVP of the recent World Series, is seen celebrating with fans during the victory parade held for the Brewers on Oct. 30. Milwaukee won this year's World Series, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)

Under this revised proposal, teams would be obligated to limit spending to a hard cap of $258.2 million US — a level that would require eight high-spending MLB teams, including the Toronto Blue Jays, to trim payroll to meet such requirements for 2028.

The owners also want teams to achieve a minimum spend of $180.2 million US — and management says 12 MLB teams, including the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers, would have to boost their payroll to reach this threshold.
'A prudent way to go'
Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro has been through labour negotiations in the sport before, and says the plan is the same this time around — cap or no cap.
Blue Jays front office speaks after end of disappointing season
"You prepare under the current system and then you adjust along the way," he told media at the end of the season.
"That's a prudent way to go," said Duquette, who served as the general manager of the Montreal Expos in the early '90s.
But Duquette said it's hard for organizations to make long-term investments — such as player contracts — if they lack certainty in what the rules are going to be in a new labour deal.

He points to a moment from the '90s, when he was in talks with the Boston Red Sox about joining their organization (which he did, leaving the Expos to become the general manager of the Red Sox, ahead of the 1994 season).

Dan Duquette is seen speaking to then-Baltimore Orioles manager Buck Showalter during spring training in February 2014. Duquette was the Orioles' executive vice-president for baseball operations. (Gene J. Puskar/The Associated Press)
Boston had plans to build up its capacity to recruit international players, but Duquette said the organization waited to make that investment until the next labour agreement was a done deal.
"When they have certainty, they can go ahead and invest," said Duquette, who also held an executive role with the Baltimore Orioles.
The flip-side of this situation is that any contractual obligations that teams have already inked with players don't go away just because a new labour agreement comes into effect.
"The obligations that the teams have made to date, those remain club obligations," said Duquette.
Free agency begins
The off-season is the time that teams can use to improve their rosters for the year to come — whether via signing free agents, trading player contracts, or through other transactions.

Starting pitcher Tarik Skubal is seen delivering a pitch for the Los Angeles Dodgers, during Game 1 of the National League Championship Series in October. Skubal is a free agent this off-season and one of the marquee pitchers available to sign. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
Some observers believe the short window of time left on the current MLB labour agreement will spur the parties involved to get things done while there is certainty about the rules of engagement.

"There's a lot of pressure, in my opinion — on the GMs, on the agents, on the players — to get transactions done," Jim Bowden, a former general manager of the Cincinnati Reds and also the Washington Nationals, told the Foul Territory podcast.
MLB's free agency period got underway late on Monday. This is the time of year when teams can sign any players who lack contractual obligations to any clubs.
In the first few days of free agency, no major free agent signings had been announced. That's not unusual for the rhythm of baseball's free agent market, which tends to pick up later in the fall.
But any fears of a potential lockout did not appear to have ignited an immediate signing frenzy.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Ombudsman: 1% of Chinese visa-free tourists overstay in Philippines
articles.summary: Around 1% of Chinese tourists who entered the Philippines visa-free in recent months did not go back home, according to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla

blocks.text: Published November 7, 2026 4:50pm
Around 1% of Chinese tourists who entered the Philippines visa-free did not go back home, according to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla.
Speaking on his radio show on DZRH, Remulla commented on the Department of Tourism’s request to the Department of Foreign Affairs to extend visa-free entry for Chinese nationals.

“Pinag-aralan na namin iyan. Yung visa-free na yan, more or less 1%, during the first two months, yung hindi na bumalik sa China. Kung 200,000 yan, may 2,000 kaagad yan. Yung nandito, TNT (tago nang tago) na yan,” Remulla said.
(We studied that. That visa-free, more or less, 1% of them, during the first two months, did not return to China. So if that is 200,000, that is already 2,000 TNT.)
Remulla reiterated earlier calls to outsource visa processing to a third-party, as the Department of Foreign Affairs was making money off of issuing visas through travel agencies.

“Ang DFA, kumikita diyan ang DFA, yung travel agencies, nagp-process ng mga visa. Ang nagsabi sa akin niyan, a very big Fil-Chi businessman in China… Nag-reklamo siya sa akin, when I was Secretary of Justice, kaya nag-away na kami niyan ni Tess Lazaro. Harap-harapan ko sinabi sa kanya ‘yan. I’m not doing this behind her back. I said it to her face,” Remulla said.
GMA News Online has reached out to the DFA for a response to Remulla’s newest comments, but it has yet to reply as of posting time.

(The DFA, the DFA is making money there, the travel agencies that process the visa. The one who told me that is a very big Fil-Chi businessman in China… he complained to me when I was Secretary of Justice, so me and Tess Lazaro have fought over that. I said it to her directly. I’m not doing this behind her back. I said it to her face.)
The same businessman supposedly told Remulla that it was easier to get a US visa for business than to get a visa in the Philippines for the same reason.
The DFA has already previously thumbed down Remulla’s calls to outsource the visa-processing to a third party. The agency also reiterated that it had no tolerance for corruption.

“The visa fees collected are pursuant to applicable laws and regulations, including the prescribed Schedule of Fees. The DFA does not tolerate corruption and remains committed to accountability, transparency, and utmost professionalism in the delivery of public service,” the agency said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to watchdog over clash with journalist
articles.summary:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

Russell Brand’s barrister has…

blocks.text: Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after his client had been found guilty of rape.
Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”
Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”
“Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court on Thursday afternoon, with a group of journalists watching.
In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator.

He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny.
“I have made such a report.”

The incident happened moments after a jury had found Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.
Brand, 51, had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.
After the trial, experts added to calls for a change in the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”.
In his closing speech, Winter said none of the complainants had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave” during their encounters with Brand.

Claire Waxman, who is the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, is seeking to update the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”. She criticised “outdated and harmful assumptions” that victims must have to have screamed or tried to fight off their attacker or immediately reported an offence.
Judges routinely issue directions cautioning juries against relying on such stereotypes. But Waxman’s office said it needed to be stated plainly in legislation to ensure consistency.
Mr Justice Bennathan, the judge in Brand’s trial, told the jury in his legal directions not to assume the delay in making complaints to the police meant the allegations were untrue.

Deniz Ugur, deputy director of the End Violence Against Women (EVAW) coalition, said: “It is really appalling to see defence lawyers intentionally lean into a whole range of tired tropes and myths about rape.
“Rape myths like the ones we’ve seen in this case have no place in the courtroom.”

The head of Scotland Yard, Sir Mark Rowley, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme he supported Waxman’s call. “I think what I’ve heard reported heads towards, it’s getting very close to victim-blaming, which is something we’ve thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don’t do.

“People fall into myths about [how] a rape victim must behave in a certain way, must react in a certain way. The evidence is really clear. Some people will fight. Some people will freeze. Some people will tell people straight away. Some people bottle it up for years. There isn’t one way of reacting.”
On Friday a No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed that Waxman’s calls should be examined.

Speaking after the trial Urwin told a Times podcast she approached Winter after the verdict because her name had been mentioned during the trial. “I thought he’s talked about me a lot, I’ll go and introduce myself and that is a legitimate thing to do,” she said. “I was surprised to be confronted and spoken to in that way.”

It is understood that several complaints have been submitted to the Bar Standards Board but the regulator said it would not “comment as to whether or not it has received any information about potential misconduct by a barrister regardless of how any information comes to our attention”.
A spokesperson said complaints were usually handled confidentially unless they resulted in a disciplinary tribunal hearing.
The comedian Katherine Ryan criticised the barrister on her podcast, Telling Everybody Everything, saying: “That was so unprofessional, so inappropriate, so aggressive. Really sickening.”

Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, defended Urwin, his newspaper’s chief news correspondent. He said: “I found what Mr Winter did quite extraordinary. I have never seen or heard of a barrister behaving in this way.
“There’s a really serious point here, which is that it was not Ros who found Russell Brand guilty at Southwark crown court.

“It was a jury of eight men and four women who have sat through this case. They’ve listened to the evidence, they’ve listened to the defence, and they have gone away and they’ve come back with some very considered verdicts.
“By impugning Ros’s integrity, what Mr Winter is doing, and he should really be called to account for this, he’s impugning the integrity of the entire case.
“He’s impugning the integrity of a jury … who have sat there solemnly and done their duty, and the judge who oversaw the case and everybody else involved. I think what he did was reprehensible.”

blocks.caption: The jury found Russell Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock

blocks.text: During the trial, Winter had argued that reporting of allegations against Brand by the Times, the Sunday Times and a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary had “poisoned the well”, and rendered it impossible for his client to have a fair trial.
The trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, dismissed an attempt by Brand to block his trial from taking place because of negative media coverage.

In a pre-trial argument, Brand, through Winter, had accused the journalists who first exposed him as a sexual predator of being “criminals”, suggesting their reporting in 2023 had made a fair trial impossible and venturing that they may have committed the crime of perverting the course of justice.
But the judge rejected that attempt to stop the trial, ruling that Brand could simply be tried by people who had not seen the previous media reporting.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.

“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths but we are going further by changing the law to stop irrelevant sexual history and previous allegations being weaponised against rape victims.
“We will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”
Brand was convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan in 2009 and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009.
He is in custody and due to be sentenced on Monday.

articles.title: BJMP told to justify Romualdez's personal aide inside cell
articles.summary: Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla has ordered the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to explain why a personal aide of Leyte Rep. and former House Speaker Ferdinand…

blocks.text: Headlines
November 7, 2026 | 4:36pm
Photo released yesterday by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology shows former House speaker Martin Romualdez being guarded at the Quezon City Jail.

MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla has ordered the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to explain why a personal aide of Leyte Rep. and former House Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez was allowed inside his detention cell.

In a statement posted on Facebook on Friday, November 6, Remulla directed the BJMP leadership to submit a comprehensive report within 48 hours detailing the legal and administrative basis for allowing the aide inside the detention cell, the circumstances surrounding the arrangement and the officials or personnel involved.
The report must include supporting records and documents and establish whether applicable laws and regulations were followed, Remulla said.

"I have said this before, and I will say it again: the law must be applied equally across all jail facilities. No position, political influence, or personal connection exempts anyone from compliance with established rules and regulations," he said.
The DILG chief said the authorization of the aide's presence inside Romualdez's detention cell warrants "immediate scrutiny and a full accounting" from the BJMP.
"Incomplete findings, unsupported explanations, and failure to comply with this directive will not be accepted," Remulla said.
Remulla also ordered the BJMP to preserve all relevant records and warned that any violations established by the investigation would be addressed promptly.

"Any official found to have exceeded that authority or violated established regulations will face appropriate administrative proceedings and, where warranted, criminal prosecution, with due process fully observed," he said.

He stressed that the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) would enforce accountability among its personnel, saying the integrity of the country's custodial institutions should not be compromised by unauthorized privileges.
"No special treatment. No selective enforcement. No one is above the law," Remulla said.
Warden explains aide's presence

The directive came after New Quezon City Jail warden Supt. Maria Lourdes Pacion confirmed before the Sandiganbayan Third Division on November 5 that Romualdez had a personal staff member staying with him inside his detention cell.
Pacion said she authorized the arrangement because Romualdez needed assistance with his daily needs and the jail could not provide additional personnel to attend to him.
"I allowed it because his mental state is not yet that stable per my assessment. We cannot hire more personnel to attend to the personal needs of Congressman Romualdez," Pacion told the court.
She also cited humanitarian considerations in allowing the arrangement, saying jail personnel could not attend to all the needs of persons deprived of liberty.
Romualdez has been detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September in connection with a P7.4-billion plunder case linked to the alleged flood control corruption scandal.

The Sandiganbayan has separately ordered jail authorities to submit a detailed report on Romualdez's whereabouts inside the facility, including CCTV footage and records of individuals authorized to assist him.
