articles.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
articles.summary: The US president's promotion of Miller, a loyal partisan firebrand to be his new chief of staff sets up likely clashes with Congress.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
By
North America correspondent
In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.
On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.
"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."
Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’

Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.

He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.

He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.
Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.

He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.

Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.

The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.
What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?
Miller's hardline views sets up clash with Congress
While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.
It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans.

"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."
Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".
The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.

Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.

blocks.caption: Stephen Miller and Donald Trump appear in the Oval Office in front of an American flag and a statue of George Washington

blocks.text: On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".
That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.

Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".
Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.

"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.

At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

articles.title: Paraguay: President Santiago Pena under house arrest over bank crisis
articles.summary: Paraguay’s Senate has ousted President Santiago Pena over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government. Millions of customers' accounts are frozen, with public pension and health care funds…

image.caption: Pena's rapid downfall came amid mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, one of the country's biggest banks, with which he had ties (FILE: 03/03/2025)Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paraguay's Senate on Friday impeached President Santiago Pena over a banking crisis that left millions of people unable to access their deposits.
Senators voted overwhelmingly to remove Pena for misconduct in office.
The move cleared the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to succeed him. He will serve the rest of the presidential term, which ends in August 2028.

Pena had already resigned on Thursday, but by impeaching and convicting him instead of accepting his resignation, senators stripped him of the lifetime Senate seat and immunity granted to former presidents, leaving him vulnerable to prosecution.
Following the Senate vote, prosecutors ordered the arrest of the ousted president alongside former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo as part of a criminal investigation.
Officials later said Pena was placed under house arrest pending a decision by the public prosecutor's office on the final charges against him.
Dozens of ​protesters gathered outside ​his residence ‌in the capital Asuncion, while police maintained ​a ⁠security cordon around the property.
Why did Pena face impeachment?
Pena's rapid downfall came amid mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, one of the country's biggest banks, with which he had ties.
The bank's accounts — also used to process pension payments — are frozen, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money. Ueno also held hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds.
Pena's resignation on Thursday followed the withdrawal of support by Congress President Basilio Nunez and ruling conservative Colorado Party leader Horacio Cartes.

Thirty-five opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents had submitted impeachment articles in the 80-seat Chamber of Deputies, accusing Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to Ueno.
Pena sold his shares in Ueno Holding, whose businesses include the bank, in April 2025. Lawmakers also cited two loans he received from Ueno as part of allegations of improper financial gain.

They alleged improper presidential interference in the Social Security Institute, known as IPS, and preferential treatment for Ueno. IPS manages pension and health care funds for most Paraguayan workers and held $355 million at the bank — about 9% of its investments, according to financial manager Gladys Vera.

The motion also questioned Pena's 2023 appointment of central bank chief Carvallo, who previously chaired Financiera Ueno. According to the document, the central bank approved the company's conversion into a bank just 83 days after his appointment.
What happened to Ueno Bank?
Ueno served about 2.94 million customers, roughly 60% of Paraguay's adult population.

As of last month, the bank said it held roughly $800 million in public-sector deposits — about a quarter of its total deposits — including money from the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

blocks.caption: People took the the streets of Asuncion on WednesdayImage: Jorge Saenz/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paraguay's central bank ordered a resolution or closure process Tuesday after finding that Ueno's solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum.
Ueno's app, card payments and transfers stopped working, while branches closed, leaving customers queuing outside unable to withdraw their savings.
Hundreds of employees of Ueno and other companies in its parent conglomerate protested outside the Labor Ministry Thursday, demanding unpaid wages and severance.
Retirees, depositors, students and workers had marched through Asuncion a day earlier, demanding Pena's impeachment and holding signs saying "Give us back our money."
What have authorities done?

Authorities detained eight senior executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank president Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud.
Lawyers for several detainees said they needed time to review the allegations before commenting.
Pena had sought to reassure customers in a video message Wednesday, pledging legislation "that will return to every saver what they are entitled to as quickly as possible."
The crisis also forced him to cancel his attendance at the Ibero-American summit in Madrid.
Pena, a conservative economist, took office in August 2023 for a five-year term.
Editor's Note: This piece, originally published on November 5, was updated on November 7 to reflect the latest developments.

articles.title: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions
articles.summary:
Primary school students bested 200,000 competitors across New South Wales to reach the Premier’s Spelling Bee finals in Sydney

  • Get our

blocks.text: Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.
At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.

All have made it past about 200,000 students who competed in spelling bees across 1,070 public schools in New South Wales. The finalists earned their place at this year’s state competition after winning online regional finals in August. They represent the top 0.03%. And they’re not here to mess around.

Five are competing for a third time, having progressed to the last stage in the junior competition. Among them are year 5 student Wafiq Ayyash from the Hunter region, who won the junior state title in 2024, and year 6 student Bobby Ivaneza from the inner west, who was runner-up the same year.

Ewan Mattick from the state’s central west, Caleb Borg from the Riverina, and Alesha Kahfandi from the Hunter have also qualified for the state finals on three occasions. This isn’t their first rodeo.

blocks.caption: The tension is palpable on stage at the 2026 NSW Premier’s Spelling Bee. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The format is relatively simple. Contestants begin with “seen” words that they’ve been able to practise at home, before facing “unseen” words testing their broader skills and composure. Each round is sudden death.
To kick off, they’re introduced to the crowd by the host, ABC presenter Rae Johnston, with colourful details.

Archie Griffith likes the Parramatta Eels and his dachshund puppy. He doesn’t like his dad’s jokes. Ivaneza, who is wearing a bright red sweatband, admires Nicola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer who died in 1943, for his genius. Ivaneza’s favourite food is camembert.
The students are as diverse as the schools they come from. Some 23 speak a language other than English at home, and 18 have travelled from outside Sydney.
Seven go down in the first round, stumbling over obscure words like “tourmaline” and “malapropism”. Another seven are out in round two – but you try spelling “lepidopterist” at home.
In the next four rounds, 13 students fall. Mattick nails “centurion” and gives a thumbs up to his family. Come round seven, Kahfandi begins to pray.
“Pernicious” and “sagacious” bring two more students down. And then there are five: Afeef Ahmed, Ivaneza, Kahfandi, Caroline Wang, and Maximilian Lumley, all in year 6. Two are returning finalists.

In round eight, they all spell their words correctly, though Ivaneza, usually breezing through with confidence, restarts on “whimsical”. Then, in round nine, he’s asked to spell “unserviceable” and omits the second “e”.

Ivaneza, visibly devastated, slumps into his seat and places his head in his hands. The remaining students spell their words correctly, and Ivaneza tearily returns to his family in the crowd and the comforting embrace of his father. The heartbreak is palpable.

Then, in an instant, after Ahmed correctly spells “immemorial”, the remaining three competitors fall. Kahfandi misses “antepenultimate”, Wang gets tied up by “parmigiana” and Lumley is one letter off getting “genealogy”. Ahmed has won.

blocks.caption: Alesha Kahfandi missed ‘antepenultimate’ but is tied for runner-up. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: But the show must go on.
after newsletter promotion

“We are in an interesting situation,” Johnston says. “We need to play for a runner up.” Wang goes out straight away after being dealt the word “grandiloquent”. But Kahfandi and Lumley appear to be in lockstep. For the next five rounds, they’re either both correct or both wrong.
“We’re just going to keep on going,” Johnston declares. It begins to feel that the audience will grow old in this theatre, steadily working its way through the entire Macquarie Dictionary.
But then, Kahfandi misses the word “vociferous”. Lumley approaches the microphone and awaits his fate. His word is “apocalypse” and, after a deep breath, he nails it.

The crowd bursts into cheers, and Lumley returns to his seat and stares reflectively at the ground, looking like he has endured a war. His grandmother, Sue, is bursting with pride. “It was so stressful,” she says, “and he looked so calm.”
“He’s worked so hard. Some of those words, I didn’t even know what they were. We’re very proud.”

blocks.caption: Maximilian Lumley wins second place in the 2026 NSW Premier’s Spelling Bee in Penrith in Sydney’s west. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Kahfandi is proud of herself, too. “It was very tense in the room, there was a lot of pressure on everyone,” she says. “I feel a bit disappointed I didn’t get second and I was a bit tired after all those rounds, but getting third place is also really good.”
Ahmed is surprised he’s won, but his mother isn’t. She’s been helping him train for months – half an hour every night before bed.
“He reads a lot,” she says. “I knew he would win; he was three-time champion at school.”
Asked how he felt when he found out he’d won Ahmed says, at first, he “didn’t realise”.
“But then when they said we had a winner, I felt happy,” he says. “The runners-up words were harder than the ones I got.”

articles.title: Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay at start of South America tour
articles.summary: Pope Leo has arrived in Uruguay at the start of a 12-day trip through three South American nations. His trip, which is intense with a packed itinerary, comes just weeks after his lung cancer surgery.

image.caption: Uruguay's President Yamandu Orsi welcomed Pope Leo as he landed in Carrasco International Airport Image: Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Uruguay on Friday at the start of a grueling 12-day tour through three South American countries, just weeks after his lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff told reporters he was very happy to be in Uruguay, having flown a nearly 14-hour flight from Rome to get to Montevideo.
"I confess that from the first day, I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward," he told reporters aboard the papal plane.
Leo hit the ground running on arrival, drawing huge crowds in Montevideo as he pulled into town in his open-sided popemobile.
The Vatican estimated 30,000 people had turned out to watch him go by and attend his first event in a country that is largely secular and where membership in the Church is declining.

"In an age ‌when ​differences can easily become a source of conflict, persevering ​in respect for the law, negotiation and the ⁠patient ​search for ​agreements is a service ​that Uruguay ‌can continue to offer its neighbors," ​Leo ⁠told crowds in Montevideo's main square.
Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance, was present there too.
Leo is then planning to visit the Casavalle neighborhood, which is notorious for its high rates of poverty and violence.
With starting in Uruguay, Leo marks the first papal visit to the country in nearly four decades, with Pope John Paul II having last visited in 1988.
What to know about Pope Leo's taxing itinerary
The pontiff will spend three days in Uruguay before heading on to Argentina on Sunday.
He then travels to Peru, where he spent half his priestly life, before he was elected pontiff last year. He became a naturalized Peruvian citizen in 2015.
Latin America is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, for whom the pope is their spiritual leader. However, fewer and fewer people on the continent identify as Catholic.
Enthusiasm around Leo's visit a surprise in Uruguay

Uruguay, the most secular Latin American country, was the first country in the world to legalize recreational marijuana use and has since legalized abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all against opposition from the Catholic Church.
However, the enthusiasm around Leo's visit has come as a bit of a surprise, with tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium selling out in just two days.

blocks.caption: The pope is expected to express opposition to some of the more liberal policies enacted in UruguayImage: Lucas Aguayo Araos/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: What will Pope Leo do in Argentina?
On Sunday, Leo will cross over to neighboring Argentina, the home of his papal predecessor Francis, who, however, disappointed his native compatriots by never returning home as pope.
At the beginning of Francis's papacy, some 71% of Argentinians identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. By 2024, this had fallen to 58%.

blocks.caption: Leo will hope his visit makes up for the refusal by his predecessor to visit his home countryImage: Agustin Marcarian/REUTERS

blocks.text: Leo is set to meet with Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has come under criticism from the Catholic Church for his sweeping cuts that have hampered programs for the poor and needy.
He is also planning to meet with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives.
Pope Leo to return to Peru for last leg of trip
The final leg of the trip, on Wednesday, will see Leo return to Peru, where he lived and preached for two decades.
There is excitement about his visit to Peru, with the pope planning to celebrate Mass in his old diocese of Chiclayo as well as in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
The pope will also celebrate Mass in the former Incan capital city of Cusco before honoring Peru's indigenous population by traveling to Pucallpa in the Peruvian Amazon.
The excitement can be seen in the street vendors selling T-shirts and rosaries with his likeness, while bakeries have been selling Leo bread.
Peru has also seen a weakening of the faithful in recent years, with the Catholic population falling from 76% in 2013-2014 to around 67% now.

blocks.caption: Peruvian Catholics have shown particular interest in the pope's visit as a type of homecomingImage: Martin Mejia/AP Photo/picture alliance

articles.title: 4 reasons to watch Canada in the women's hockey world championship
articles.summary: Here are four reasons why it's worth paying attention to the Canadian women in this year's hockey world championship

image.caption: Canada's players celebrate their first goal goal score by Jessie Eldridge (9) during the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship Group B game between Sweden and Canada in Herning, Denmark, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Here are four reasons why it's worth paying attention to the Canadian women in this year's hockey world championship
Canada has shaken up the team at every level after some heartbreaking losses

Yes, there's the patriotism of cheering for your country, and yes, there's the Canada/U.S. rivalry, but those aren't the only reasons to watch Team Canada in the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship.
Canada dominated Sweden 5-1 in its world women's hockey championship opener Friday to kick off the 11-day, 10-nation tournament in Denmark. Their next game is Sunday, when they face Japan.
The U.S. and Canada are the tournament favourites, continuing a long-standing cross-border rivalry. Canada has won 13 world titles followed by the U.S. with 11 spanning the previous 24 championships.
But this year, there are even more reasons it's worth paying attention to the Canadian team. Here are a few of them:
Jesse Eldridge leads Canada past Sweden at the worlds
1. The youngest lineup in decades
To quote Hockey Canada's Women's Worlds preview, "the kids have arrived."

The average age of this roster is 26 years, two months and 22 days — the youngest roster Canada has played at the Women’s Worlds since 2013, Hockey Canada notes. Three of the youngest players are debuting in Denmark: Rosalie Tremblay (age 18), Hayley McDonald (age 18), and Sara Manness (age 19).

items: 7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth

blocks.text: Three other collegiate players, 19-year-old Chloe Primerano (University of Minnesota), 20-year-old Caitlin Kraemer (University of Minnesota Duluth) and 23-year-old Ève Gascon (University of Minnesota Duluth) return for their second world championship.
The oldest player is goaltender Ann-Renée Desbien, who is 32.

Canada's goalkeeper Ann-Renée Desbien makes a save during the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship Group B game between Sweden and Canada in Herning, Denmark on Friday. (Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix/The Associated Press)
2. Poulin is out
Hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin has been sidelined due to knee surgery after tearing her ACL last spring, leaving the Canadian team without its captain for the first time in more than a decade.

Poulin is widely regarded as one of the greatest women's hockey players of all time. She's won three Olympic gold medals, scoring the winning goal in all three of those gold-medal games to earn the nickname "Captain Clutch."

items: What to know for the women's hockey world championship
7 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth

blocks.text: A five-time Olympian, Poulin is also the all-time leading goal scorer for the Canadian women's team at the Winter Games with 20. With her out, Canada is playing in its first international tournament without Poulin on the roster since she made her national team debut in 2009.
Defender Renata Fast and forward Laura Stacey are sharing Canada's captaincy in Denmark.
Hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin provides update about her health
3. New head coach and management
The Canadians ended last season with a heartbreaking loss in the Olympic gold-medal game against the Americans. Since then, there's been change at all levels for Canada.

The group has new leadership, starting with Hockey Hall of Famer Danièle Sauvageau, who returns to the Hockey Canada fold as GM of the senior national team. Ottawa Charge GM Mike Hirshfeld and PWHL Detroit GM Manon Rhéaume are serving as assistant GMs.

items: Mix of young, veteran players invited to Canadian women's hockey team camp

blocks.text: There's also a new head coach: Kori Cheverie, who led Sauvageau's Victoire to a Walter Cup in the spring. Cheverie has been an assistant with the national team since before the 2022 Olympic gold-medal win.

Montreal Victoire head coach Kori Cheverie hoists the Walter Cup alongside general manager Daniele Sauvageau during the Montreal Victoire's victory celebration in Montreal in May. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
4. Coming off some big losses

The Americans have won 10 of the past 14 worlds and claimed the 2025 title in the Czech Republic and the Olympic gold medal at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, beating Canada in overtime in both finals.
Canada was also swept in the Canada/U.S. Rivalry Series that concluded last December. So now, with a fresh roster and without its greatest star, Canada is looking to reclaim the championship.

The final is set for Nov. 16. While it's not necessarily guaranteed that Team Canada will make it, it's been Canada vs. the U.S. in 23 out of the last 24 finals. The lone exception came in 2019, when host Finland shocked the Canadians in the semis before losing a controversial final against the States.
With files from CBC's Karissa Donkin and Jesse Campigotto, Reuters and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Restaurant owner defends planned ban on children under 15 amid backlash
articles.summary: The chef and owner of a Jamaican restaurant set to open in Winnipeg's West End at the end of this month is facing both backlash and support for her decision to exclude some children from its dine-in…

image.caption: The owner of Miss Christine's Kitchen on Ellice Avenue, expected to open this month, plans to only serve people age 15 and older. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

The chef and owner of a Jamaican restaurant set to open in Winnipeg's West End at the end of this month is facing both backlash and support for her decision to exclude some children from its dine-in experience.
Lawyer says case for discrimination depends on circumstances, negative outcomes experienced by complainant
Christine Pattison recently posted on social media that she plans to only allow people age 15 and older at Miss Christine's Kitchen on Ellice Avenue.
Pattison received swift criticism, she said in an interview on Information Radio with guest host Cory Funk on Friday.
She said she has been accused of breaking the law and discriminating against children.
Pattison's goal is to create a quiet and intimate experience that would be disrupted or ruined by kids running around and screaming, she said.
"Personally, I think it's a great idea," said Pattison, who has seven grandchildren, age four to 21.
"I want to give [customers] a space where they can come without their kids and have a wonderful evening, because it's so cozy and nice in there."
Christine Pattison, the chef and owner of Miss Christine's Kitchen, says some parents don't adequately control their children, making dining at restaurants less enjoyable. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)
Guests will be welcomed on a reservation basis, and the restaurant won't have a kids' menu, high chairs or a changing table.
"If anyone says that their kids never drive them crazy, they are a big fat liar."
Pattison decided to go this direction because of bad experiences at her previous restaurant, where children were permitted.
"That's all fine, but for this space, I wanted to create something special for adults only," she said.

Pattison feels her decision was somewhat validated after a visit by two of her grandchildren, age four and six. They left taps on in the washroom, played with burning candles and ran around dragging things, she said.
Pattison isn't surprised by the backlash but said many people have emailed her messages of support.
Legality 'depends': lawyer
One attorney who practises human rights law said businesses must comply with Manitoba's human rights code, which includes not discriminating based on age and family status.

While the code doesn't establish a test for proving discrimination, case law does, said Joëlle Pastora Sala, who works with the Public Interest Law Centre in Winnipeg, in conversation with host Marjorie Dowhos on Radio Noon.

Pastora Sala said she is not involved in the case at Miss Christine's Kitchen and her comments are not legal advice, but an often-cited legal decision in British Columbia said to prove discrimination, complainants have to show they suffered adverse impacts from a policy.
"Once you've done that, then the establishment — or the restaurant, in this case — would have to justify … the alleged discrimination," Pastora Sala said.
Joëlle Pastora Sala, a lawyer with the Public Interest Law Centre, say generally speaking, determining illegal discrimination depends on a number of factors. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)
In other words, the restaurant would have to justify that the age they identified is rationally connected to the service, she said.
Pastora Sala could not speak to whether Pattison's reasons were "justifiable enough."
"The classic … answer would be that it depends," she said.
It would depend on the age identified, the circumstances and the negative outcomes that a complainant suffered, Pastora Sala said.
If businesses are found to have violated human rights, the courts may offer various remedies, including financial compensation.

items: Years-long waits for human rights complaint hearings in Manitoba point to 'broken' system, lawyer says

blocks.text: Businesses may also be directed to change policies and undergo training.

Pattison said she has called the Manitoba Human Rights Commission to see if her plan violates human rights, but she didn't immediately connect with anyone. She expects a response within five to 10 days.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rosanna Hempel is a multiplatform journalist with a background in biology and forestry. She has been with CBC Manitoba since 2023, covering everything from extreme weather, health and housing to issues affecting Indigenous communities. She previously worked at CJOB/Global Winnipeg, where she was part of a team recognized by the Radio Television Digital News Association for its coverage of the 2023 Carberry bus crash. She speaks French and German. You can email her at rosanna.hempel@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US change course
articles.summary: Despite an ostensible deal between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin to bring diesel to the US, tankers are reportedly unable to dock due to existing sanctions.

image.caption: In October, Trump said 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel would be released to global marketsImage: Yoruk Isik/REUTERS

blocks.text: Several sanctioned tankers headed for the US carrying Russian diesel are said to have changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to data from marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com.
The tankers reportedly departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month and had declared their destinations as the US east coast.

This all comes after US President Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian oil last month, in a deal with with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to secure a large amount of diesel directly to the US at a time when diesel prices have skyrocketed across the country.
The agreement caused shock and drew criticism in Ukraine and Europe. But it also was a logistical challenge, given that sanctions against Russia still remain in place.
It was also widely reported at the time that the amount of diesel in question was a fraction of the US daily demand.
Russia says reports are 'fake'
UK newspaper The Financial Times (FT) reported Wednesday that two of the tankers appeared to have changed their destination and were no longer headed to the United States.
Russian envoy and negotiator Kirill Dmitriev said on Thursday that the US-bound diesel tankers were still on course.
"Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course," Dmitriev said on X, linking to the FT story.
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said detail of shipments were a "commercial" matter that could not be made public.
"All diesel will find its buyers," he added, without elaborating.
A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the US but changed its destination from New York to a vague "for orders," without listing an unloading point.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
NJ governor threatens 'harsh penalties'

Despite the fact that the US Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill warned port and terminal operators to turn away ships carrying the fuel.
In a letter earlier this week, she warned that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”
Sherrill accused the Trump administration of lacking authority in overriding the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago.
She said New Jersey would act to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel.
In a letter dated October 27, Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal warned shipping companies against violating US sanctions forbidding imports of Russian fuel.
"No president can unilaterally override a statute. Trump's license will not absolve you of legal and moral accountability," the letter read.

articles.title: Stephen Miller named by Trump as new White House chief of staff
articles.summary: Trump said he would be replacing Susie Wiles for the top advisory role. Miller is controversial figure, known as a key architect of the administration's hardline immigration policies.

image.caption: Steven Miller is a long-time member of Trump's inner circleImage: Aaron Schwartz/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: US President Donald ‌Trump announced on ⁠Friday ⁠that his ​deputy chief of ​staff and architect of his administration's strict immigration policy, Stephen Miller, will become his new chief of staff.
Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who had been in the post since Trump's inauguration. With the nod, Miller becomes the top aide to the president.
Trump announced the move, saying Miller was "one of my most trusted advisors," adding that Wiles has done an outstanding job, and would be "moving over" to the "Trump political operation."
"He gets it" and is "very good politically. And he's a very good man. He'll do a great job, great manager," Trump said.
Wiles also commented on her exit from the White House, saying that her work there was "the honor of a lifetime."
The move comes after Trump's Republican Party lost control of the House and Senate after a midterm election rout at the hands of Democrats.
One of Trump's longest-serving aides
The 41-year-old is one of Trump's longest-serving advisers, having joined Trump's longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter.
Although his portfolio as deputy chief of staff was wide-ranging, Miller is most responsible for Trump's policies and rhetoric on immigration.
Miller's appointment is a signal that Trump intends to continue on with his hardline immigration policies, despite voters rejecting Republicans around the country.
Miller is known for taking controversial positions, and is one of the Trump administration's most vocal advocates, frequently making media appearances to defend extreme positions.
Miller a controversial figure

On immigration, his ideas have included calling for federal agents to make 3,000 arrests every day, while allowing the agency to target migrants who have lived in the US for decades. He is widely created with helping expand the remit of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations

On foreign policy, Miller has defended extrajudicial strikes on boats in Caribbean Sea allegedly used by drugs smugglers, and defended the administration's military operation to snatch Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January.
In January 2026, Miller went on broadcaster CNN and claimed that the US had the right the seize Greenland, after Trump said controlling the Danish territory was a strategic necessity.

"We live in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world since the beginning of time," Miller told CNN's host Jake Tapper.
Miller also has not held back on attacking the administration's opponents.
During the midterm campaign, Miller called Democrats "extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics" on social media.
He also promoted claims about election fraud in California and Alaska, which were not substantiated.

As Trump has lost control of both chambers of Congress, Miller has been credited with working in the background to create an obstructionist strategy for the White House to block Democratic legislation. Trump has taken to the strategy and has said, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto."
Democrats vow to 'fight' Miller's agenda

After Trump's announcement, New York Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who could become the next speaker of the House, posted on social media that Miller was a "dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," referring to the deaths of US citizens protesting ICE raids.
Senator Chuck Schumer issued a statement saying the Trump had "learned nothing" after the Republican's election drubbing.
"Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration," said Schumer, who is positioned to become the next Senate majority leader in January.
"Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way," he said.
US actions in Venezuela reflect Trump's 'strength' rhetoric

articles.title: Tesla will stop making Cybertrucks next year: Musk
articles.summary: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival…

image.caption: New Tesla Cybertrucks are seen at SpaceX's Starship facility in Starbase, Texas, on Oct. 13. (Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.
Shift comes after years of weak sales

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk's pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker's autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.
Furthermore, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion US in combined market capitalization for the week.
A Tesla Cybertruck near the White House last year. (Leah Millis/Reuters)

While it wasn't immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialized components for the heavy, angular model.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."
Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

items: Elon Musk gets little bang for his buck in U.S. midterms, with possible Democratic investigations to come

blocks.text: The U.S. EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. last year, down 48 per cent from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.
"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."
"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."
Musk's SpaceX was one of the model's biggest customers last year and bought $131 million worth of Cybertrucks from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.
Tesla unveils electric Cybertruck, smashes its 'bulletproof' glass
'Cybertruck won't go, can't go'

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.
The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them — only to leave massive cracks in two of them.
During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.
Elon Musk shows off redesigned Tesla Roadster that can thrust itself into the air
Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the U.S. market.
"All of them lost the competition because electric pickups aren't popular in the U.S.," Munoz said.

But Cybertruck's sharp-edged, stainless steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe, where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.
"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.

articles.title: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
articles.summary:
The Chilean film-maker, whose films starred Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore and Rachel Weisz, died at his home in Santiago

Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of…

blocks.text: Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.
He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.

His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram without specifying the cause of death but telling followers, in Spanish, that it was a painful time for his family. Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.

Lelio was born in Argentina but moved to Chile at the age of two. He studied journalism for one year before graduating from film school and then released 9/11 documentary Cero in 2003. His first narrative film The Sacred Family premiered at the San Sebastián film festival in 2005.

His follow-up, 2009’s Christmas, premiered at Cannes but it was 2013’s Gloria that provided him with a major international breakthrough. The drama, about a woman in her late 50s who starts dating again, premiered at Berlin and won its lead star Paulina García an acting award at the festival.

Lelio followed it up with A Fantastic Woman, a drama about the life of a trans woman, another breakout that became the first Chilean film to win the Oscar for best international feature. In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a sublime study in the exalted ordeal of grief”.

“When we released it in 2017, a gender identity bill had been dormant in congress for seven years,” he said in a Guardian interview in 2018. “Somehow, the film’s release, and the year in which it became globally known, helped to reactivate the discussion in Chile.”

He made his English language debut with London-set drama Disobedience which told a queer love story between women played by Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams. It was nominated for five British independent film awards.

Lelio then remade Gloria as Gloria Bell, then set in America and starring Julianne Moore in the lead role. He followed it with a critically acclaimed adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel The Wonder starring Florence Pugh.

“I love working with actors, and need to know they trust me and can explore, get lost, be foolish or brave, and I’ll take care of them,” he said to the Guardian. “I love working on set – it is where the sparkle is.”
His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.
“Making a film is like a gift you leave somewhere – you then hide and see what happens,” he said.

articles.title: Trump replaces chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller after midterm defeat
articles.summary: Just days after the Republican Party's resounding defeat in the midterms, U.S. President Donald Trump is replacing his top political adviser, chief of staff Susie Wiles, with immigration hardliner…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles as his top political adviser at the White House. Miller, seen here in the Oval Office on Aug. 6, has been Trump's deputy chief of staff for policy and is the key architect of the administration's immig

blocks.text: World

Just days after the Republican Party's resounding defeat in the midterms, U.S. President Donald Trump is replacing his top political adviser, chief of staff Susie Wiles, with immigration hardliner Stephen Miller.
Move announced in social media post brings immigration hardliner into top White House role

Just days after the Republican Party's resounding defeat in the midterm elections, U.S. President Donald Trump is replacing his top political adviser, chief of staff Susie Wiles, with immigration hardliner Stephen Miller.
Trump announced Wiles's departure from the White House in a post on Truth Social.
He called Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers and said Miller — the deputy chief of staff and architect of the administration's mass deportation push — would take over the top job on Monday.
"I wanted to make a change," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Friday afternoon.
"Sometimes in life you have to make moves," he said. "Stephen's been with me from the beginning and he gets it."
Political observers say Miller's elevation signals Trump has no intention of backing away from the key policies that have defined his second term, despite the midterms drubbing.
Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles out after midterm defeat
That includes the mass deportation campaign that has gone far beyond its promised target of the worst criminals.

Backlash against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detentions of undocumented immigrants who've lived upstanding lives in the U.S. for years was one of the factors that swung many Hispanic voters against the Republicans in the midterms, helping to deliver a Senate seat for Texas to Democrat James Talarico.
Seen as a Trump loyalist

Marc Short, who served as White House director of legislative affairs in Trump's first term, says he expects Miller to bring a combative approach to the new political balance of power in Washington which sees Democrats in control of Congress.
"It's hard for the president to find somebody more loyal to him than Stephen has been," Short told CNN on Friday.
"You're going to have an executive branch versus a legislative flight that's coming, and I think that the White House wants that fight."
Democrats are reacting to Miller's appointment as a sign that Trump has no plans to moderate his agenda.
Trump defends Hegseth as Democrats prepare for political war
"Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat," the Democrat leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, said in a statement.
"Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice," Schumer said.
'Tripling down on MAGA insanity'
Tommy Vietor, a former Obama administration spokesperson, described Trump's move as "tripling down on MAGA insanity."
"Great way to signal that you learned zero lessons from the midterm debacle," Vietor said in a post on X.
The American Immigration Council, a Washington, D.C., non-profit that advocates for immigrant rights, called Miller the architect of Trump's "most harmful" immigration policies.

"It’s clear that Trump, despite receiving a decisive rebuke of his policies on Election Day, plans to double down on the extreme immigration agenda we’ve seen these last two years," the group's executive director Jeremy Robbins said in a statement Friday.
"Stephen Miller is behind the worst of the worst: the Muslim Ban. Family Separation. Masked ICE agents killing people in the streets," Robbins said.

U.S. President Donald Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles, seen here on Oct. 9 in Washington, is leaving the top political post in the White House. Trump made the announcement in a post on Truth Social and said her replacement will be Stephen Miller. (Tom Brenner/The Associated Press)
Miller's appointment so soon after the election is being seen as part of Trump's search for scapegoats for the scale of the midterm defeat.
The Democrats won the popular vote for House seats by 13 percentage points, the widest margin for any party since 1976.
Wiles is one of the people Trump is blaming, CNN reported Friday, citing unnamed sources in the administration.
For much of the past year, Wiles had signalled that Trump would campaign for the midterms with a focus on affordability.

However the president instead sent voters an inconsistent message — often dismissing concerns about the cost of living while spending significant time in his rally speeches talking about his construction projects in Washington, D.C.
In his social media post, Trump said Wiles had done an outstanding job and will be "moving over to the Trump Political Operation."
Trump shrugs off midterm blowout as blame game kicks off

It was not immediately clear what Trump means by his "political operation." It could be his MAGA Inc. political action committee, a fundraising organization that had hundreds of millions of dollars at its disposal to back Republican candidates in the midterms and could prove influential in the 2028 presidential campaign.
In her own post on X, Wiles did not specify what her new job would be.
"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she wrote.

items: Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?
Trump's Justice Department hit by 2 high-profile departures this week

blocks.text: Her departure is the latest in a series of high-profile women exiting the Trump administration.

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Attorney General Pam Bondi, Labour Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard either resigned or were ousted earlier this year.
Karoline Leavitt stepped down as White House press secretary in August.

Leavitt called Miller the perfect choice for chief of staff. "No one is more loyal, more hardworking, or more in touch with the America First movement than Stephen," she said Friday afternoon in a post on X.
"Now is the time to fix what's not working and double down on all of the victories we've already achieved," Leavitt wrote.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam
articles.summary:
Separate actions also take place outside fence and across Europe in backlash against impact of AI boom

Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as…

blocks.text: Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.

Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.

The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.

The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.

“The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used,” the police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster. “An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”

Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.

Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.

Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands, but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.

“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”

The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.

Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacenter is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”
after newsletter promotion

A spokesperson for Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration and that its first concern was the wellbeing of everyone at and around the site. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully. However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
A spokesperson for Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected the right to peaceful protest but that entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous.

“Our immediate priority is everyone’s safety, and we respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have,” a Pure DC spokesperson said.

Governments across Europe have supported the building of AI datacentres to boost tax revenues and catch up with the breakneck deployment of computing power in the US and China, with some framing the AI race as a matter of national security.

But datacentres have emerged as a flashpoint for public anger over issues from environment and energy to human rights and democracy. Last week, an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe found evidence of dangerous conditions for some of the workers building them.

articles.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
articles.summary: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide…

image.caption: Ilse Aigner is the speaker of Bavaria's parliament, and reportedly the front-runner for a joint Christian Democrat nomination to be the next German president [FILE: October 24, 2026]Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU, want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.
It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.

But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel, the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.
DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.
On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.

blocks.caption: Aigner appears to have the backing of both Bavaria's Markus Söder and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, visible in the background on the main stage at the CSU party conference in this photoImage: Peter Kneffel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's first woman as president?

If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.
She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.
Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.
Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.
She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.

blocks.caption: Aigner is the speaker or president of Bavaria's state parliament at present, she's also a former federal agriculture minister Image: Rolf Poss/IMAGO

blocks.text: What steps remain on the path to Germany picking a new president?
The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats (SPD), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.

"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.
A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.
It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.
Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.
The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.

Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.
This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.

articles.title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
articles.summary: Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people.

blocks.text: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.

Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.

The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

articles.title: Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck
articles.summary: Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive…

image.caption: A Cybertruck might be parked at sites like Tesla's Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg, but the vast pickup is not road legal in Germany [FILE: April 23, 2026]Image: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.
"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

blocks.caption: Cybertrucks fit on LA's wide roads with relative ease, but that's not the case everywhereImage: Barry King/Alamy/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why did the Cybertruck fail to attract customers?
Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."
For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."
However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.
Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.
Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.
Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

blocks.caption: The agressive set-square design appealed to some of the more eccentric and well-financed police departments in the US like casino capital Las VegasImage: Ty ONeil/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How far short of Musk's sales targets did the Cybertruck fall?
Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.
But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.
At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.
For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

blocks.caption: SpaceX purchased a vast fleet of Cybertrucks in 2025, perhaps feeling the futuristic styling fits the company's aesthetics, or perhaps as a favor to a friendImage: Charles Briggs/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the story with the next pet project, the Cybercab?
The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.
Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

blocks.caption: Tesla held a Cybercab launch party in Ausitin in September this yearImage: Bob Daemmrich/ZUMA/picture alliance
