articles.title: Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston
articles.summary:
Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado

Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern…

blocks.text: Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73.4F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth also spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were the result on an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.

Further south in the US, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather impacting polling stations in states such Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms this week even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing a relocation of the polling station. The tornado left extensive damage across the town, although no causalities have been reported. Officials across many states impacted by the severe weather have requested federal funding assistance after extreme weather resulted in widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.

Across the Atlantic, a number of authorities in the Mediterranean regions of southern France, Corsica and Sardinia issued severe flood warnings this week, as an area of low pressure in the region brought thunderstorms and torrential rain. As much as 50-100mm (2-4in) of rain is expected over the coming days with more localised totals in excess of 100mm possible in the southern French regions of Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur and Occitanie, as well as Corsica. Where torrential rain is most prolonged, up to 70-80mm of rain could fall within a 24-hour period. Further rain is expected next week as low pressure continues to dominate the weather pattern in the region.

articles.title: When patients learn they may not have MS after all, it's rarely a relief. Instead, they have more questions
articles.summary: Experts and patients say MS misdiagnosis can happen as researchers continue to improve their understanding of the disease and develop better ways to diagnose it.

image.caption: Multiple sclerosis misdiagnoses can happen, as researchers learn more about the complex condition and develop better ways to diagnose it. But for patients who were previously told they had MS, finding out they don't isn't always a relief. (Father - Studio/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: LISTEN | What happens when you find out you don't have multiple sclerosis:
The Current24:07When you find out you don’t have MS after all
More than 20 years after she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, Jackie Pilon learned something she never expected: she didn't have the disease after all.
“I remember walking away feeling shocked, lost, hurt,” Pilon, who lives in Saskatoon, told The Current's guest host Catherine Cullen.
Pilon was 21 when she was diagnosed with MS in 1992, after what she describes as a “very thorough investigation” by her doctors.

At the time, she couldn’t see out of her right eye, a result of optic neuritis — an inflammation of the optic nerve. She started experiencing seizures and other cognitive and behavioural changes, due to encephalitis — a swelling of the brain tissue — and was hospitalized under the care of a neurologist.
This combination of symptoms led doctors to diagnose her with MS, a conclusion she says made sense based on the medical knowledge and diagnostic criteria available at the time.
But in 2016, Pilon was told she didn’t meet the updated criteria for the condition, scoring 0 for 3.
More than two decades after she was diagnosed with MS, Jackie Pilon learned that she didn't have the condition. (Submitted by Jackie Pilon)
Her experience is not uncommon.

A U.S. study by Cedars-Sinai researchers in 2019 found nearly one in five of the 241 MS patients studied had been misdiagnosed, while a 2024 review of six studies published in the Multiple Sclerosis Journal estimated an overall misdiagnosis rate of 15 per cent, with individual studies suggesting it could range from five to 41 per cent.
In late October, American actress Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with MS, which she said left her frustrated and searching for answers about her symptoms.
Pilon felt similar frustration and recalled moving through the “stages of grief.”

She had spent a considerable amount on medications she may not have needed, including injections every other day that would sometimes have flu-like side effects, like body aches and fatigue, she said. The side effects were sporadic and ended when she stopped the injections.
And she had ongoing questions, and struggled with losing part of her identity.
“It was a sense of, well, ‘What did I have and what happened?’”
Why MS can be difficult to diagnose

Multiple sclerosis is a chronic disease that affects the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves. It happens when the immune system mistakenly attacks myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibres, damaging it and disrupting the signals travelling between the brain and the body.
Symptoms can vary and may include fatigue, headaches, vision problems, slurred speech, difficulty moving, numbness and memory problems.

items: UBC researcher suggests multiple sclerosis may develop earlier than people think

blocks.text: Getting a diagnosis, while emotional, gives people an explanation for their symptoms and treatment options to manage them, says Julie Fiol, the director of clinical content strategy at the National Multiple Sclerosis Society.
If that’s overturned, patients are not always relieved, she said — instead, it can often create more uncertainty.
“When you lose that diagnosis, you start back at Square 1,” she said. “You have anxiety and stress and potentially depression around having to start this journey over again.”

Julie Fiol is the director of clinical content strategy at the National MS Society and a member of the society's research and medical affairs team. She also has a background in MS nursing and social work. (Submitted by Julie Fiol)
The reason MS can be misdiagnosed, Fiol said, is that its symptoms “really overlap with many other neurological conditions — and other types of conditions.”

“There is no one test that can confirm that someone has MS,” she said. “To be able to give someone a diagnosis more quickly and more accurately … is to [have] more tests that are more specific — or tell us there’s really no better explanation other than MS.”
One of the main tools for diagnosis, says Fiol, is an MRI, which looks for damage to the myelin sheath.

The latest diagnostic criteria, updated in 2024, include “imaging biomarkers” within the areas of damage that are specific to MS. These include the central vein sign, a small vein running through the centre of a lesion, and paramagnetic rim lesions, which appear as a ring around the edge of certain lesions on an MRI.
Those same diagnostic tests are also revealing that people with a previous diagnosis actually don't have the condition, Fiol said.

New data around paramagnetic rim lesions will likely be included in the next update of the criteria, says Fiol, which could potentially help patients get an earlier diagnosis, and provide greater accuracy.
How often are people misdiagnosed?
The evolution of the diagnostic criteria for MS has inspired more study into the accuracy of past diagnoses.

Dr. Jiwon Oh, a neurologist and medical director of the Barlo Multiple Sclerosis Program at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, has conducted research around misdiagnosis and found the rate to be 10 to 20 per cent — figures that she said should be “a wake-up call for clinicians.”
“It's not common, but it's also not exceedingly rare,” Oh said.
Researchers are still “trying to unravel all of [the] puzzle pieces” of what causes MS, she said.
Dr. Jiwon Oh is a neurologist and MS specialist based out of St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto. (Oliver Walters/CBC)
The disease, for example, is more common in countries farther from the equator, she said, a pattern researchers have linked in part to lower sunlight exposure and vitamin D levels.
Research has also linked Epstein-Barr virus to MS, though infection alone is not enough to cause the condition.

items: New findings 'strongly suggest' Epstein-Barr virus may help trigger multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: Finding a way forward after misdiagnosis

If people find out that they’ve been misdiagnosed, they should get in touch with their doctor or nurse practitioner to investigate what might be causing their symptoms, Fiol said — and whether they should be seen by a specialist.
And she encourages them to lean on family, friends and other support networks.
That can include the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, she said, which has online and peer support to “navigate the complex health-care landscape,” Fiol said.

items: Learning to embrace life with multiple sclerosis: How this N.L. woman is coping with change
This man is biking across Canada to raise $1M and break barriers for those with multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: Pilon got her rediagnosis after she started having severe migraines. Doctors ordered MRIs to investigate their cause, and the results raised questions about her MS diagnosis.

Instead, her doctor said he believed she had a condition called acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) based on reviewing her medical reports from the original diagnosis, though he couldn't be certain. ADEM is typically episodic and, for most patients, will only happen once and causes sudden inflammation of the central nervous system.
But she continues to advocate for people living with MS.

“I would just say to everyone, ‘Do what you think is right for you: ask the questions, be proactive in your health,” she said. “And if you're capable and able, invest in research, support researchers around the community [and] participate in studies.”

articles.title: Global stocks plunge amid AI slowdown fears after Democrats’ midterm triumph
articles.summary: Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.5%

blocks.text: European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, with the FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, down 1.5%, or 166 points, at the start of trading to 10,615.

The pharmaceuticals company AstraZeneca opened down 2.8%, the biggest faller on the FTSE 100. Other big fallers included IAG, the owner of British Airways and Iberia, which fell 1.5%, after it missed profit forecasts in a trading update, and the miners Antofagasta and Anglo American.
Germany’s Dax index opened down 1.5%, France’s Cac 40 has dropped by 1.2% and Spain’s Ibex is down 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8% in early trading.
Despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
after newsletter promotion
The Nasdaq Composite index, for example, is still up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

articles.title: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis
articles.summary:
Santiago Peña’s rightwing administration had authorised Ueno Bank to drastically expand operations before collapse

Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a…

blocks.text: Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.

At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.

Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.
In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.

“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.

Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.

The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.

The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.

Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.
Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.

“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.
Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.
“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.

“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.

Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case “the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era … This is a bank created from political power, to use public money for private businesses linked to political power, with the president of the republic at the head of it,” he told 1020 AM radio.

Peña, a former finance minister who promised to rebuild a “great Paraguay”, was a key ally of the US president, Donald Trump, in the region – one of the few Latin American presidents to attend Trump’s second inauguration. US officials, including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, repeatedly praised him as a “strategic partner”, and Peña recently flew to Washington to discuss critical minerals and economic cooperation. Neither Rubio nor Trump has yet commented on Peña’s resignation.
Vice-President Pedro Alliana automatically assumes the presidency to complete the constitutional term until August 2028.

About an hour after Peña’s announcement, the lower house unanimously approved the impeachment motion, which now goes to the senate. If approved, even after his resignation, he would lose his senate seat and, with it, parliamentary immunity, leaving him to face any criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

articles.title: Bomb hoaxes: Messages reveal how threat was passed on by air traffic control
articles.summary: BBC Verify has been analysing messages after flights across Europe were targeted by fake bomb threats - the second such incident this week.

blocks.text: More than 20 aircraft across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats. It's the second time this week, which the UK has called a "malicious hoax".
BBC Verify has been analysing the messages sent by an aircraft to find out what happens when a flight receives a bomb hoax - as Thomas Copeland explains.
Additional reporting by Emma Pengelly. Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Sally Nicholls.

articles.title: Herzog to meet Israeli election rivals as decision nears on path to power
articles.summary:
President calls on all parties to help avoid new election after Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs fell short of majority

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, was due to meet Benjamin Netanyahu and…

blocks.text: Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, was due to meet Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, on Thursday with less than a week left before he decides which of the two men should first try to form a government.

A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.

Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.

The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.
“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.

Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.

Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.
Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.

“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility ​rests upon us,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu remains prime minister ​in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another ‌election, which must be held if no candidate ‌succeeds.

Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on ​an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast ​doubt on the results, accusing Israeli Palestinian-led parties of stealing ​the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.

Israel’s Central Election Committee said ​on Wednesday that the election’s integrity ‌had not been compromised. The ​head of the committee, the supreme court justice ​Noam Sohlberg, has called on the country’s elected officials to protect public trust.

“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. He said high voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far right, including Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

articles.title: Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half brother ‘person of interest’ in child sexual abuse inquiry
articles.summary:
Philippine authorities say there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but was not being treated as a suspect

The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half brother,…

blocks.text: The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.
The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.

He added that Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.
More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.
He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.
Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US where he is now living.
Remulla said: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.”
He added: “We will know in the next few days.”

Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.
Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.
Markle Jr reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.

Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.

Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.

articles.title: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report
articles.summary:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors

The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts…

blocks.text: The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.
A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.

The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education.

The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of popular groups BTS and Katseye) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”.
In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe representatives said the company adheres to child-protection laws and works hard to make sure its artists work and train in safe conditions.

NewJeans are one of the decade’s most popular K-pop acts. In 2023, the five-member group followed Blackpink to become the second Korean girl-group to score a number one album on the Billboard charts. In November 2024, the band made global headlines when they announced their decision to leave the label amid contract disputes and claims that Ador had deliberately undermined their careers.
Band member Hanni alleged that NewJeans were mistreated by the label and accused Ador of “deliberate miscommunications and manipulation” in a statement to South Korea’s parliament last year.

Ador has consistently maintained that they did not violate their duty. “A unilateral claim that trust has been broken does not constitute valid grounds for termination of a contract,” the label said in a statement.
The label sued band member Danielle, a member of her family and the band’s producer in December 2025 for a total of nearly $30m for damages and a contract break penalty.
Hybe representatives told the New York Times that its exit penalty fees do not exceed industry standards.
In July, the group promised that 2026 would be the “summer of NewJeans,” with a teaser showing the group as a four-piece sans Danielle. New music has yet to emerge.
The new reports expose the shadowy world of K-pop contracts and shine a light on the restrictive conditions that the genre’s biggest stars can be subject to.

By the time they signed their contracts, the NewJeans members – Minji, Hanni, Haerin, Hyein and Danielle – had already clocked in years of training in K-pop “boot camps” which taught vocal training, choreography and foreign language education.
Schedules were strict, one source told the New York Times, and it was not unusual for rehearsals to stretch as late as 2am. NewJeans’s youngest member, Hyein, was 12 at the time.

After the band members received their exclusive contracts with Ador in January 2022, the parents of one member requested multiple changes. They were told that the “contract itself” could be reconsidered if it was not signed in its current form.
In a statement to the New York Times, Hybe said its contracts were legal and negotiated in good faith, with protections in place for the artist as well as the label’s investment in them.

That contract also struck government language that forbade performers working for “excessive periods of time”. It also stipulated that the band would have to repay a significant percentage of the plastic surgery costs that are common in K-pop.
“We do not even recommend cosmetic surgery or procedures against an individual’s wishes,” Hybe said in a statement.

The NewJeans contact also granted Ador rights to use the band members’ “name, photographs, likeness, handwriting, voice and any other elements” in perpetuity, in a level of ownership that goes further than government recommendations for such rights to end at the point of contract termination.
The clause also grants Ador the right to use the NewJeans members as AI chatbots or clones.
The Guardian has reached out to Hybe for comment.

articles.title: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war
articles.summary:
Dismissals follow Houthi victories and pressure from southern Yemenis for more power

The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt…

blocks.text: The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.

A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
Reuters reported on Monday that Houthi forces were only about 37 miles (60km) from Aden, the nominal seat of the UN-recognised government.
A burst of government dismissals and appointments reflects military reverses and possibly a perceived need to be more sensitive to the demands of southern Yemenis.

Between 1967 and 1990, the country was divided in two, and there is a strong movement built around the banned Southern Transitional Council (STC) seeking to revert to that division, or create a more federated country.
The government has become dependent on southern troops to fend off Houthi advances, but these forces insist they will fight only to defend land inside former South Yemen.

Fresh claims were also aired this week that STC leaders were coerced by the Saudis into dissolving the organisation against their will. The growing criticism of Saudi Arabia from STC officials in the media reflects their confidence that if the north is lost to the Houthis, the Saudis will have to let the STC operate openly. Not all southern separatists support the STC, an organisation that overreached itself in January, making it easier for the Saudi leadership to defer decisions on the southern question.

Some of the most senior figures in the UN-backed government are largely based in hotels in Riyadh rather than operating permanently from inside Yemen and the government is dependent on Saudi money to pay salaries. Critics say the administration has become a “hotel government”.

Earlier this week, its ruling executive – the presidential leadership council – met for the first time in months in Riyadh, where it addressed the loss of swathes of territory to the Houthis along Yemen’s west coast. Since then, the fighting has moved into the mountains around Taiz.

In an attempt to rebalance the north-south divide in his government, President Rashad al-Alimi sacked the long-serving information minister, Muammar al-Eryani, replacing him with Prof Salem al-Awlaki, previously a minister for the civil service and a spokesperson for the STC from 2017 to 2019. Alimi chose two other southerners as ministers for local administration and the civil service and appointed new leaders for the civil aviation authority, the ports of Aden and the ministry of transport.

blocks.caption: Camels in besieged Taiz, which is the third largest city in Yemen. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters

blocks.text: He also sacked Yusuf al-Sharaji, the military figure responsible for the Taiz front and Abu Bakr al-Jabouli, a brigadier responsible for the Tor al-Baha axis. Widespread accusations had been made about al-Sharaji’s failure to manage operations, resulting in the fall of several areas and districts to the Houthis.
The task of lifting the siege of Taiz and coordinating forces has been handed to Maj Gen Rashad al-Yousfi, a career officer.

Part of the difficulty is the tension between the different forces fighting on the government’s side. It has been claimed that Abu Zara’a, the leader of the Southern Giants, has fallen out with the Homeland Shield Forces, which are funded by Saudi Arabia and affiliated with Abdulrahman al-Lahji.

The Homeland Shield experienced heavy losses, leading al-Lahji to file an official report accusing Abu Zara’a of treason, and warning that the situation in Dhubab, close to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, had become extremely dangerous for the government. Repeated claims that control of the strait had been wrested back from the Houthis were contradicted by the evidence.

articles.title: Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
articles.summary: The chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".

blocks.text: Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.
It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.

articles.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola to be evacuated from DRC to UK, document shows
articles.summary:
Patient, who is ⁠in ​stable condition, is expected to arrive in Britain on Wednesday or Thursday

A British healthcare worker infected with Ebola ⁠is being medically evacuated from the…

blocks.text: A British healthcare worker infected with Ebola ⁠is being medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Britain for specialist treatment, according to an official document seen by ⁠Reuters.

The patient is ⁠in a ​stable condition and is expected to arrive in Britain on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred to a specialist ambulance to ⁠a high-consequence infectious disease unit, the document showed.
It quoted British authorities saying they did not expect the case to have a serious public health ⁠impact in Britain, and anticipated no disruption to international travel or trade.

“A British citizen currently ​in the DRC has tested positive for ‌Ebola,” a spokesperson for ‌Britain’s government told Reuters in an emailed statement. “ … The risk to the UK public ‌from Ebola remains low.“
The patient, whose identity was not disclosed, had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help support the response to the outbreak.
It is the first case involving a British national linked to the current outbreak, although several other people from elsewhere in Europe have been infected.

Switzerland last month evacuated an Ebola patient ‌from Nigeria for treatment, while France in June reported its first confirmed case tied to the outbreak in a doctor returning from a humanitarian ​mission in DR Congo.

Ebola is a severe viral disease spread through direct contact with an infected person’s body fluids. The World Health Organization says the disease is fatal in about half of cases on average, though mortality rates vary between outbreaks.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the ​National Health Service has procedures ​in place to manage suspected ​and confirmed infections.
Imported cases are rare, with only four confirmed cases recorded in ​Britain since 1976, ‌according to the ​UK Health Security Agency.
The ​outbreak in DR Congo is the second-largest on record, with more than 10,000 confirmed cases and nearly 5,000 deaths reported by late October.
